description:
Introduction

This Highway Code applies to England, Scotland and Wales. The Highway Code is essential reading for everyone.

The aim of The Highway Code is to promote safety on the road, whilst also supporting a healthy, sustainable and efficient transport system.

Wording of The Highway Code

Many of the rules in the Code are legal requirements, and if you disobey these rules you are committing a criminal offence. You may be fined, given penalty points on your licence or be disqualified from driving. In the most serious cases you may be sent to prison.

Such rules are identified by the use of the words ‘MUST/MUST NOT’. In addition, the rule includes an abbreviated reference to the legislation which creates the offence. See an explanation of the abbreviations.

Although failure to comply with the other rules of the Code will not, in itself, cause a person to be prosecuted, The Highway Code may be used in evidence in any court proceedings under the Traffic Acts (see The road user and the law) to establish liability. This includes rules which use advisory wording such as ‘should/should not’ or ‘do/do not’.

Knowing and applying the rules

Knowing and applying the rules contained in The Highway Code could significantly reduce road casualties. Cutting the number of deaths and injuries that occur on our roads every day is a responsibility we all share. The Highway Code can help us discharge that responsibility.

Further information on driving and riding techniques can be found in ‘The Official DVSA Guide to Driving - the essential skills’ and ‘The Official DVSA Guide to Riding - the essential skills’.

category: The Highway Code. 1. Introduction
description:
Self-driving vehicles

By ‘self-driving vehicles’, we mean those listed as automated vehicles by the Secretary of State for Transport under the Automated and Electric Vehicles Act 2018.

To check if your vehicle is self-driving, visit ‘Self-driving vehicles listed for use in Great Britain’.

These vehicles are capable of safely driving themselves when the self-driving function is correctly turned on and the driver follows the manufacturer’s instructions. While the vehicle is driving itself, you do not need to monitor it.

Self-driving vehicles differ from vehicles that are fitted only with assisted driving features, such as cruise control and lane-keeping assistance. Assisted driving features can do some of the driving, but the driver still needs to be responsible for driving at all times. If you are driving a vehicle using only its assisted driving features, Rule 150 applies.

A self-driving vehicle’s ability to drive itself may be limited to certain situations or parts of a journey. Things such as the type of road, time of day, weather, location and speed may affect this. You should follow the manufacturer’s instructions about when and how to use the self-driving function safely.

While a self-driving vehicle is driving itself in a valid situation, you are not responsible for how it drives. You may turn your attention away from the road and may also view content through the vehicle’s built-in infotainment apparatus, if available.

But you MUST still follow all relevant laws:

• You MUST be fit to drive. For example, you must be within the drink-drive legal limits and not be under the influence of drugs. See Rules 90 to 96.

• The vehicle MUST be road legal. For example, it must have an MOT certificate, if applicable, and it must be taxed and insured.

• The vehicle must be roadworthy. See Rules 89 and 97, ‘Motor vehicle documentation and learner driver requirements’, and ‘Vehicle maintenance, safety and security’.

• You will still be responsible for your passengers and anything else you are carrying. See Rules 98 to 102.

• You MUST NOT do anything illegal, such as using a handheld mobile phone or similar hand-held device. Exceptions to this are set out in Rule 149.

If a self-driving vehicle needs to hand control back to the driver, it will give you enough warning to do this safely. You MUST always be able and ready to take control, and you MUST do so when the vehicle prompts you. For example, you should stay in the driving seat and stay awake.

When you have taken back control or turned off the self-driving function, you are responsible for all aspects of driving.

Laws: RTA sections 2, 3, 4, 5, 5A, 14 and 15; AEVA section 1; and CUR regulations 100, 104, 109 (as modified by the Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) (Automated Vehicles) Order 2022) and 110, as amended by CUR(A) (No. 2) Regulations 2022.

category: The Highway Code. 1. Introduction
description:
Hierarchy of Road Users

The ‘hierarchy of road users’ is a concept that places those road users most at risk in the event of a collision at the top of the hierarchy. The hierarchy does not remove the need for everyone to behave responsibly.

The road users most likely to be injured in the event of a collision are pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders and motorcyclists, with children, older adults and disabled people being more at risk. The following H rules clarify this concept.

Rule H1

It is important that ALL road users:

• are aware of The Highway Code
• are considerate to other road users
• understand their responsibility for the safety of others.

Everyone suffers when road collisions occur, whether they are physically injured or not. However, those in charge of vehicles that can cause the greatest harm in the event of a collision bear the greatest responsibility to take care and reduce the danger they pose to others. This principle applies most strongly to drivers of:

• large goods and passenger vehicles
• vans and minibuses
• cars and taxis
• motorcycles.

Cyclists, horse riders and drivers of horse-drawn vehicles likewise have a responsibility to reduce danger to pedestrians.

None of this detracts from the responsibility of ALL road users, including pedestrians, cyclists and horse riders, to have regard for their own safety and the safety of other road users.

Always remember that the people you encounter may have impaired sight, hearing or mobility, and that this may not be obvious.

Rule H2

Rule for drivers, motorcyclists, horse-drawn vehicles, horse riders and cyclists.

At a junction, you should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road into which or from which you are turning.

You MUST give way to pedestrians on a zebra crossing, and to pedestrians and cyclists on a parallel crossing. See Rule 195.

Pedestrians have priority when on a zebra crossing, on a parallel crossing or at light-controlled crossings when they have a green signal.

You should give way to pedestrians waiting to cross a zebra crossing, and to pedestrians and cyclists waiting to cross a parallel crossing.

Horse riders should also give way to pedestrians on a zebra crossing, and to pedestrians and cyclists on a parallel crossing.

Cyclists should give way to pedestrians on shared-use cycle tracks and to horse riders on bridleways.

Only pedestrians may use the pavement. Pedestrians include wheelchair and mobility scooter users.

Pedestrians may use any part of the road and use cycle tracks as well as the pavement, unless signs prohibit pedestrians.

Rule H2: Wait for the pedestrian to cross the junction before turning. This applies whether you are turning right or left into the junction.

Laws: TSRGD Schedule 14, parts 1 and 5; HA 1835 section 72; R(S)A 1984 section 129; and Countryside Act 1968, section 1, part 30.

Rule H3

Rule for drivers and motorcyclists.

You should not cut across cyclists, horse riders or horse-drawn vehicles going ahead when you are turning into or out of a junction, changing direction or changing lane, just as you would not turn across the path of another motor vehicle. This applies whether they are using a cycle lane, using a cycle track or riding ahead on the road. You should give way to them.

Do not turn at a junction if doing so would cause a cyclist, horse rider or horse-drawn vehicle going straight ahead to stop or swerve.

You should stop and wait for a safe gap in the flow of cyclists if necessary. This includes when cyclists are:

• approaching, passing or moving off from a junction
• moving past or waiting alongside stationary or slow-moving traffic
• travelling around a roundabout.

Rule H3: Wait for the cyclist to pass the junction before turning. This also applies if there is a cycle lane or cycle track and whether you are turning right or left into the junction.

category: The Highway Code. 2. Rules for pedestrians (1 to 35)
description:
General guidance (Rules 1 to 6)

Rule 1

Pavements and footways, including any path along the side of a road, should be used if provided. Where possible, avoid being next to the kerb with your back to the traffic. If you have to step into the road, look both ways first.

Always remain aware of your environment and avoid unnecessary distractions. Always show due care and consideration for others.

Rule 2

If there is no pavement, keep to the right-hand side of the road so that you can see oncoming traffic. You should take extra care and:

• be prepared to walk in single file, especially on narrow roads or in poor light
• keep close to the side of the road.

It may be safer to cross the road well before a sharp right-hand bend so that oncoming traffic has a better chance of seeing you. Cross back after the bend.

Rule 3

Help other road users to see you. Wear or carry something light-coloured, bright or fluorescent in poor daylight conditions.

When it is dark, use reflective materials, for example armbands, sashes, waistcoats, jackets or footwear. Reflective materials can be seen by drivers using headlights up to three times as far away as non-reflective materials.

Rule 4

Young children should not be out alone on the pavement or road. See Rule 7.

When taking children out:

• keep between them and the traffic
• hold their hands firmly
• strap very young children into pushchairs or use reins.

When pushing a young child in a buggy, do not push the buggy into the road when checking whether it is clear to cross, particularly when emerging from between parked vehicles.

Rule 5

Organised walks or parades involving large groups of people walking along a road should use a pavement if one is available. If a pavement is not available, they should keep to the left.

Look-outs should be positioned at the front and back of the group. They should wear fluorescent clothes in daylight and reflective clothes in the dark.

At night:

• the look-out at the front should show a white light
• the look-out at the back should show a red light
• people on the outside of large groups should also carry lights and wear reflective clothing.

Rule 6

Motorways

Pedestrians MUST NOT be on motorways or slip roads except in an emergency. See Rules 272 and 277.

Laws: RTRA section 17; MT(E&W)R regulation 15(1)(b); and MT(S)R regulation 13.

category: The Highway Code. 2. Rules for pedestrians (1 to 35)
description:
Crossing the road (Rules 7 to 17)

Rule 7

The Green Cross Code

The advice below on crossing the road is for all pedestrians. Children should be taught the Code and should not be allowed out alone until they can understand and use it properly. The age when they can do this is different for each child.

Many children cannot judge how fast vehicles are travelling or how far away they are. Children learn by example, so parents and carers should always use the Code in full when out with their children. Parents and carers are responsible for deciding at what age children can use it safely by themselves.

A. First find a safe place to cross

Find somewhere safe to cross and where there is space to reach the pavement on the other side. Where there is a crossing nearby, use it.

It is safer to cross using:

• a subway
• a footbridge
• an island
• a zebra crossing
• a pelican crossing
• a toucan crossing
• a puffin crossing
• a crossing point controlled by a police officer, school crossing patrol or traffic warden.

Otherwise, choose a place where you can see clearly in all directions. Try to avoid crossing:

• between parked cars — see Rule 14
• on a blind bend
• close to the brow of a hill.

Move to a space where drivers and riders can see you clearly. Do not cross the road diagonally.

B. Stop before the kerb

Stop just before you reach the kerb, where you can see whether anything is coming. Do not get too close to the traffic. If there is no pavement, keep back from the edge of the road while making sure you can still see approaching traffic.

C. Look and listen

Look all around for traffic and listen. Traffic could come from any direction. Listen as well as looking because you can sometimes hear traffic before you see it.

D. Let approaching traffic pass

If traffic is coming, let it pass. Look all around again and listen. Do not cross until there is a safe gap in the traffic and you are certain there is plenty of time. Remember that even traffic a long way away may be approaching very quickly.

E. Cross safely

When it is safe, go straight across the road and do not run. Keep looking and listening for traffic while crossing in case there is traffic you did not see or other traffic appears suddenly.

Look out for cyclists and motorcyclists travelling between lanes of traffic. Do not walk diagonally across the road.

Rule 8

At a junction

When you are crossing or waiting to cross the road, other traffic should give way. Look out for traffic turning into the road, especially from behind you, and cross at a place where drivers can see you.

If you have started crossing and traffic wants to turn into the road, you have priority and the traffic should give way. See Rules H2 and 170.

Rule 9

Pedestrian safety barriers

Where there are barriers, cross the road only at the gaps provided for pedestrians. Do not climb over the barriers or walk between them and the road.

Rule 10

Tactile paving

Raised surfaces that can be felt underfoot provide warning and guidance to blind or partially sighted people.

The most common surfaces are:

• a series of raised studs, used at crossing points with a dropped kerb
• a series of rounded raised bars, used at level crossings, at the top and bottom of steps and at some other hazards.

Rule 11

One-way streets

Check which way the traffic is moving. Do not cross until it is safe to do so without stopping. Bus and cycle lanes may operate in the opposite direction to the rest of the traffic.

Rule 12

Bus and cycle lanes

Take care when crossing bus and cycle lanes because traffic may be moving faster than in the other lanes or against the flow of traffic.

Rule 13

Routes shared with cyclists

Cycle tracks may run alongside footpaths or pavements and be separated from them by a feature such as:

• a change of material
• a verge
• a kerb
• a white line.

These routes may also incorporate short lengths of tactile paving to help visually impaired people remain on the correct side.

On the pedestrian side, the tactile paving may comprise a series of flat-topped bars running across the direction of travel, known as the ladder pattern. On the cyclist side, the same bars are orientated in the direction of travel, known as the tramline pattern.

Some routes shared with cyclists are not separated by such a feature, allowing cyclists and pedestrians to share the same space. Cyclists should respect your safety — see Rule 62 — but you should also take care not to obstruct or endanger them. Always remain aware of your environment and avoid unnecessary distractions.

Where signs indicate, some routes are shared between pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles. Cyclists, horse riders and drivers of horse-drawn vehicles should respect your safety, but you should take care not to obstruct or endanger them. Always remain aware of your environment and avoid unnecessary distractions.

Rule 14

Parked vehicles

If you have to cross between parked vehicles, use the outside edges of the vehicles as if they were the kerb. Stop there and make sure you can see all around and that traffic can see you.

Make sure there is a gap between any parked vehicles on the other side so that you can reach the pavement.

Never cross the road in front of or behind any vehicle with its engine running, especially a large vehicle, because the driver may not be able to see you.

Rule 15

Reversing vehicles

Never cross behind a vehicle that is reversing, showing white reversing lights or sounding a warning.

Rule 16

Moving vehicles

You MUST NOT get onto or hold onto a moving vehicle.

Law: RTA 1988 section 26.

Rule 17

At night

Wear something reflective to make it easier for others to see you. See Rule 3.

If there is no pedestrian crossing nearby, cross the road near a street light so that traffic can see you more easily.

category: The Highway Code. 2. Rules for pedestrians (1 to 35)
description:
Crossings (Rules 18 to 30)

Rule 18

At all crossings

When using any type of crossing, you should:

• always check that traffic has stopped before you start to cross or push a pram onto the crossing
• always cross between the studs or over the zebra markings.

Do not cross at the side of the crossing or on the zig-zag lines, as this can be dangerous.

You MUST NOT loiter on any type of crossing.

Laws: TSRGD Schedule 14, Part 5, and RTRA section 25(5).

Rule 19

Zebra crossings

Give traffic plenty of time to see you and stop before you start to cross. Vehicles will need more time to stop when the road is slippery.

Wait until traffic has stopped in both directions or the road is clear before crossing. Remember that traffic does not have to stop until someone has moved onto the crossing.

Drivers and riders should give way to pedestrians waiting to cross and MUST give way to pedestrians on a zebra crossing. See Rule H2.

Keep looking both ways and listening in case a driver or rider has not seen you and attempts to overtake a vehicle that has stopped.

Zebra crossings have flashing beacons.

A zebra crossing with a central island is two separate crossings. See Rule 20.

Law: TSRGD Schedule 14, Part 5.

Rule 20

Where there is an island in the middle of a zebra crossing, wait on the island and follow Rule 19 before crossing the second half of the road. It is a separate crossing.

Rule 21

At traffic lights

There may be special signals for pedestrians. You should start to cross the road only when the green figure shows.

If you have started crossing and the green figure goes out, you should still have time to reach the other side, but do not delay.

If no pedestrian signals are provided, watch carefully and do not cross until the traffic lights are red and traffic has stopped.

Keep looking and check for traffic that may be turning the corner. Remember that traffic lights may allow traffic to move in some lanes while traffic in other lanes has stopped.

Rule 22

Pelican crossings

Pelican crossings are signal-controlled crossings operated by pedestrians. Push the control button to activate the traffic signals.

When the red figure shows, do not cross. When a steady green figure shows, check that traffic has stopped and then cross with care.

When the green figure begins to flash, you should not start to cross. If you have already started crossing, you should have time to finish safely.

Rule 23

Puffin crossings

Puffin crossings differ from pelican crossings because the red and green figures are above the control box on your side of the road, and there is no flashing green figure phase.

Press the button and wait for the green figure to show.

Rule 24

Congested roads

When the road is congested, traffic on your side may be forced to stop even though its lights are green. Traffic may still be moving on the other side of the road, so press the button and wait for the signal to cross.

Rule 25

Toucan crossings

Toucan crossings are light-controlled crossings that allow cyclists and pedestrians to share the crossing space and cross at the same time. They are operated by push button.

Pedestrians and cyclists see the green signal together. Cyclists are permitted to ride across.

Rule 26

Signals for people with sensory impairments

At some crossings, there is a bleeping sound or voice signal to indicate to blind or partially sighted people when the steady green figure is showing. There may also be a tactile signal to help deafblind people.

Rule 27

Equestrian crossings

Equestrian crossings are for horse riders. They have:

• pavement barriers
• wider crossing spaces
• horse and rider figures in the light panels
• either two sets of controls, one of which is higher, or one higher control panel.

Rule 28

Staggered pelican or puffin crossings

When the crossings on each side of the central refuge are not in line, they are two separate crossings. On reaching the central island, press the button again and wait for a steady green figure.

Rule 29

Crossings controlled by an authorised person

Do not cross the road unless you are signalled to do so by a police officer, traffic warden or school crossing patrol. Always cross in front of them.

Rule 30

Crossing where there are no controlled crossing points

Where no controlled crossing points are available, it is advisable to cross where there is an island in the middle of the road.

Use the Green Cross Code — see Rule 7 — to cross to the island. Stop on the island and use the Green Cross Code again to cross the second half of the road.

category: The Highway Code. 2. Rules for pedestrians (1 to 35)
description:
Situations needing extra care (Rules 31 to 35)

Rule 31

Emergency vehicles

If an ambulance, fire engine, police vehicle or other emergency vehicle approaches using flashing blue lights, headlights and/or sirens, keep off the road.

Rule 32

Buses

Get on or off a bus only when it has stopped to allow you to do so. Watch out for cyclists when you are getting off.

Never cross the road directly behind or in front of a bus. Wait until it has moved off and you can see clearly in both directions.

Rule 33

Tramways

Tramways may run through pedestrian areas. Their path will be marked out by:

• shallow kerbs
• changes in the paving or other road surface
• white lines
• yellow dots.

Cross at designated crossings where provided. Elsewhere, treat trams as you would other road vehicles and look both ways along the track before crossing.

Do not walk along the track, as trams may come up behind you. Trams move quietly and cannot steer to avoid you.

Rule 34

Railway level crossings

You MUST NOT cross or pass a stop line when the red lights show, including when a red pedestrian figure is displayed.

Do not cross if:

• an alarm is sounding
• the barriers are being lowered.

The tone of the alarm may change if another train is approaching.

If there are no lights, alarms or barriers, stop, look both ways and listen before crossing.

A tactile surface comprising rounded bars running across the direction of pedestrian travel may be installed on the footpath approaching a level crossing to warn visually impaired people of its presence. The tactile surface should extend across the full width of the footway and should be located at an appropriate distance from the barrier or the projected line of the barrier.

Law: TSRGD Schedule 14, Part 1.

Rule 35

Street and pavement repairs

A pavement may be closed temporarily because it is not safe to use. Take extra care if you are directed to walk in or cross the road.

category: The Highway Code. 3. Rules for users of powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters (36 to 46)
subcategory: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters (rules 36 to 37)
englishSubcategory: Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters (rules 36 to 37)
description:
Powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters (Rules 36 to 37)

Rule 36

There is one class of manual wheelchair, called a Class 1 invalid carriage, and two classes of powered wheelchairs and powered mobility scooters.

Manual wheelchairs and Class 2 vehicles:

• have an upper speed limit of 4 mph (6 km/h)
• are designed to be used on pavements.

Class 3 vehicles:

• have an upper speed limit of 8 mph (12 km/h)
• are equipped to be used on the road as well as the pavement.

Rule 37

When you are on the road, you should obey the guidance and rules for other vehicles. When you are on the pavement, you should follow the guidance and rules for pedestrians.

category: The Highway Code. 3. Rules for users of powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters (36 to 46)
description:
On pavements (Rules 38 to 40)

Rule 38

Pavements are safer than roads and should be used when available.

You should give pedestrians priority and show consideration for other pavement users, particularly those with a hearing or visual impairment who may not be aware that you are there.

Rule 39

Powered wheelchairs and scooters MUST NOT travel faster than 4 mph (6 km/h) on pavements or in pedestrian areas.

You may need to reduce your speed to adjust to other pavement users who may not be able to move out of your way quickly enough, or where the pavement is too narrow.

Law: UICHR regulation 4.

Rule 40

When moving from the pavement onto the road, you should take special care. Before moving off, always look around and make sure it is safe to join the traffic.

Always try to use dropped kerbs when moving off the pavement, even if this means travelling farther to locate one.

If you have to climb or descend a kerb:

• always approach it at right angles
• do not try to negotiate a kerb higher than the vehicle manufacturer recommends.

category: The Highway Code. 3. Rules for users of powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters (36 to 46)
description:
On the road (Rules 41 to 46)

Rule 41

You should take care when travelling on the road because you may be travelling more slowly than other traffic. Your machine is restricted to 8 mph (12 km/h) and may be less visible.

Rule 42

When on the road, Class 3 vehicles should travel in the direction of the traffic.

Class 2 users should always use the pavement when it is available. When there is no pavement, they should use caution when travelling on the road. Where possible, Class 2 users should travel in the direction of the traffic.

If you are travelling at night, when lights MUST be used, you should travel in the direction of the traffic to avoid confusing other road users.

Law: UICHR regulation 9.

Rule 43

You MUST follow the same rules about using lights, indicators and horns as other road vehicles if your vehicle is fitted with them.

At night, lights MUST be used.

Be aware that other road users may not see you. You should make yourself more visible, even during the daytime and at dusk, by measures such as:

• wearing a reflective jacket
• placing reflective strips on the back of the vehicle.

Law: UICHR regulation 9.

Rule 44

Take extra care at road junctions. When going straight ahead, check that there are no vehicles about to:

• cross your path from the left
• cross your path from the right
• overtake you and turn left.

There are several options for dealing with right turns, especially when turning from a major road. If moving into the middle of the road is difficult or dangerous, you can:

• stop on the left-hand side of the road and wait for a safe gap in the traffic
• negotiate the turn as a pedestrian by travelling along the pavement and crossing the road between pavements where it is safe to do so.

Class 3 users should switch their vehicles to the lower speed limit when travelling on pavements.

If a junction is too hazardous, it may be worth considering an alternative route.

Similarly, when negotiating major roundabouts with two or more lanes, it may be safer to use the pavement or find a route that avoids the roundabout altogether.

Rule 45

All normal parking restrictions should be observed.

Your vehicle should not be left unattended if it causes an obstruction to other pedestrians, especially those using wheelchairs.

Parking concessions provided under the Blue Badge scheme — see Further reading — apply to vehicles displaying a valid badge.

Rule 46

These vehicles MUST NOT be used on motorways. See Rule 253.

They should not be used on unrestricted dual carriageways where the speed limit exceeds 50 mph (80 km/h). If they are used on these dual carriageways, they MUST have a flashing amber beacon.

A flashing amber beacon should be used on all other dual carriageways. See Rule 220.

Laws: RTRA sections 17(2) and 17(3), and RVLR regulations 17(1) and 26.

category: The Highway Code. 4. Rules about animals (47 to 58)
description:
Horse-drawn vehicles (Rules 47 to 48)

Rule 47

Horse-drawn vehicles used on the highway should be operated and maintained in accordance with the standards set out in the Department for Transport’s Code of Practice for Horse-Drawn Vehicles.

This Code:

• sets out the requirements for a road driving assessment
• includes a comprehensive list of safety checks to ensure that a carriage and its fittings are safe and in good working order.

A Local Authority may require an operator to meet the standards set out in the Road Driving Assessment if the operator wishes to obtain a local authority licence to operate a passenger-carrying service.

Rule 48

Safety equipment and clothing

All horse-drawn vehicles should have two red rear reflectors.

It is safer not to drive at night. If you do drive at night, a light showing white to the front and red to the rear MUST be fitted.

Law: RVLR regulation 4.

category: The Highway Code. 4. Rules about animals (47 to 58)
description:
Horse riders (Rules 49 to 55)

Rule 49

Safety equipment

Children under the age of 14 MUST wear a helmet that complies with the Regulations. It MUST be fastened securely. Other riders should also follow these requirements.

These requirements do not apply to a child who is a follower of the Sikh religion while wearing a turban.

Laws: H(PHYR)A section 1 and H(PHYR)R regulation 3.

Rule 50

Other clothing

You should wear:

• boots or shoes with hard soles and heels
• light-coloured or fluorescent clothing in daylight
• reflective clothing if you have to ride at night or in poor visibility.

Rule 51

At night

It is safer not to ride on the road at night or in poor visibility. If you do:

• wear reflective clothing
• ensure your horse has reflective bands above the fetlock joints
• fit a light showing white to the front and red to the rear, with a band, to your right arm and/or leg or riding boot.

If you are leading a horse at night:

• carry a light in your right hand that shows white to the front and red to the rear
• wear reflective clothing on both yourself and your horse.

It is strongly recommended that your horse also wears a fluorescent or reflective tail guard.

Riding

Rule 52

Before taking a horse or horse-drawn vehicle onto the road, you should:

• ensure that all tack fits well and is in good condition
• make sure that you can control the horse.

If you are an inexperienced horse rider or have not ridden for a while, consider taking the Ride Safe Award from the British Horse Society. The Ride Safe Award provides a foundation for any horse rider to be safe and knowledgeable when riding in all environments, particularly on the road. For more information, see www.bhs.org.uk.

Always ride with other, less nervous horses if you think your horse will be nervous of traffic.

Never ride a horse without both a saddle and bridle.

Rule 53

Before riding off or turning, look behind you to make sure it is safe and then give a clear arm signal.

When riding on the road, you should:

• keep to the left
• keep both hands on the reins unless you are signalling
• keep both feet in the stirrups
• not carry another person
• not carry anything that might affect your balance or become tangled in the reins
• keep a horse you are leading on your left
• move in the direction of the traffic flow on a one-way street
• never ride more than two abreast
• ride in single file on narrow or busy roads and when riding around bends.

Rule 54

You MUST NOT take a horse onto a footpath or pavement. You should not take a horse onto a cycle track.

Use a bridleway where possible.

Equestrian crossings may be provided for horse riders to cross the road, and you should use them where available. See Rule 27.

You should dismount at level crossings where a ‘horse rider dismount’ sign is displayed.

Laws: HA 1835 section 72 and R(S)A section 129(5).

Rule 55

Avoid roundabouts wherever possible. If you use a roundabout, you should:

• keep to the left
• watch for vehicles crossing your path to leave or join the roundabout
• signal right when riding across exits to show that you are not leaving
• signal left just before leaving the roundabout.

category: The Highway Code. 4. Rules about animals (47 to 58)
description:
Other animals (Rules 56 to 58)

Rule 56

Dogs

Do not let a dog go onto the road on its own.

Keep a dog on a short lead when walking on:

• a pavement
• a road
• a path shared with cyclists or horse riders.

Rule 57

Animals in vehicles

When travelling in a vehicle, make sure dogs and other animals are suitably restrained so that they cannot:

• distract you while you are driving
• injure you if you stop quickly
• injure themselves if you stop quickly.

Ways of restraining animals in cars include:

• a seat belt harness
• a pet carrier
• a dog cage
• a dog guard.

Rule 58

Animals being herded

Animals being herded should be kept under control at all times.

If possible, send another person along the road in front to warn other road users, especially at a bend or the brow of a hill.

It is safer not to move animals after dark. If you do move them after dark:

• wear reflective clothing
• ensure that lights are carried, with a white light at the front and a red light at the rear of the herd.

category: The Highway Code. 5. Rules for cyclists (59 to 82)
description:
Overview (Rules 59 to 72)

Rule 59

Clothing

Avoid clothes that may become tangled in the chain or a wheel, or obscure your lights while cycling.

Light-coloured or fluorescent clothing can help other road users see you in daylight and poor light. Reflective clothing and accessories, such as belts and arm or ankle bands, can increase your visibility in the dark.

You should wear a cycle helmet that:

• conforms to current regulations
• is the correct size
• is securely fastened.

Evidence suggests that a correctly fitted helmet will reduce your risk of sustaining a head injury in certain circumstances.

Rule 60

At night, your cycle MUST have:

• a lit white front light
• a lit red rear light
• a red rear reflector
• amber pedal reflectors if it was manufactured after 1 October 1985.

White front reflectors and spoke reflectors will also help you to be seen.

Flashing lights are permitted, but cyclists riding in areas without street lighting are advised to use a steady front lamp.

Law: RVLR regulations 13, 18 and 24.

Rule 61

Cycle routes and other facilities

Cycle lanes are marked by a white line, which may be broken, along the carriageway. See Rule 140.

Use facilities such as cycle lanes and tracks, advanced stop lines and toucan crossings where they make your journey safer and easier. See Rules 62 and 73. Whether to use them will depend on your experience, skills and the situation at the time.

Although these facilities are provided for safety, cyclists may exercise their judgement and are not obliged to use them.

Rule 62

Cycle tracks

Cycle tracks are routes for cyclists that are physically protected from or located away from motor traffic, except where they cross side roads. See Rule 206.

Cycle tracks may run alongside footpaths or pavements and be separated from them by:

• a change of material
• a verge
• a kerb
• a white line.

You MUST keep to the side intended for cyclists because the pedestrian side remains a pavement or footpath.

Some cycle tracks shared with pedestrians are not separated by such a feature. On these shared-use routes, always take care when passing pedestrians, especially children, older people and disabled people, and allow them plenty of room. Always be prepared to slow down and stop if necessary. See Rule H2.

Law: HA 1835 section 72.

Rule 63

Sharing space with pedestrians, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles

When riding where sharing with pedestrians, horse riders or horse-drawn vehicles is permitted:

• take care when passing pedestrians and horse riders, especially children, older adults and disabled people
• slow down when necessary
• let them know you are there, for example by ringing your bell or calling out politely.

It is recommended that a bell be fitted to your cycle.

Remember that pedestrians may be deaf, blind or partially sighted, and this may not be obvious.

Do not pass pedestrians, horse riders or horse-drawn vehicles closely or at high speed, particularly from behind. You should not pass a horse on its left. Horses can be startled if passed without warning. Always be prepared to slow down and stop when necessary.

Rule 64

You MUST NOT cycle on a pavement.

Laws: HA 1835 section 72 and R(S)A section 129.

Rule 65

Bus lanes

Most bus lanes may be used by cyclists where signs indicate this.

Watch for people getting on or off a bus. Be very careful when overtaking a bus or leaving a bus lane because you will be entering a busier traffic flow.

Do not pass between the kerb and a bus when the bus is at a stop.

Rule 66

You should:

• avoid actions that could reduce your control of your cycle
• be considerate of other road users when riding in groups
• not ride close behind another vehicle in case it stops suddenly
• not carry anything that could affect your balance or become tangled in the wheels or chain
• be particularly considerate of blind and partially sighted pedestrians and horse riders — see Rule H1
• let other road users know you are there when necessary, for example by calling out or ringing your bell if you have one.

It is recommended that a bell be fitted.

You may ride two abreast, and it can be safer to do so, particularly in larger groups or when accompanying children or less-experienced riders. Be aware of drivers behind you and allow them to overtake when you feel it is safe, for example by moving into single file or stopping.

Rule 67

You should:

• look all around to ensure it is safe before moving away from the kerb, pulling out to overtake or pass stationary vehicles, turning at junctions or stopping
• watch for road obstructions such as drains, service covers and potholes
• position yourself so that you can move to the left as well as to the right to avoid obstructions safely
• take care when passing parked vehicles, leaving at least a door’s width or 1 metre to avoid being struck by an opening door
• watch for pedestrians stepping into your path
• be aware of traffic approaching from behind, including other cyclists
• give a clear signal to show other road users what you intend to do — see ‘Signals to other road users’
• take extra care near road humps, narrowings and other traffic-calming features.

When cycling on the road, pass to the left of large vehicles only when they are stationary or moving slowly. Proceed with caution because the driver may not be able to see you. Be especially careful when approaching junctions or where a large vehicle could change lanes to the left.

Rule 68

You MUST NOT:

• carry a passenger unless your cycle was built or adapted to carry one
• hold onto a moving vehicle or trailer
• ride in a dangerous, careless or inconsiderate manner
• ride while under the influence of drink or drugs, including medicine.

Law: RTA 1988 sections 24, 26, 28, 29 and 30, as amended by RTA 1991.

Rule 69

You MUST obey all traffic signs and traffic-light signals.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 3, Part 3; Schedule 7, Part 4; Schedule 9, Parts 4 and 6; Schedule 13, Part 6; and Schedule 14, Part 2.

Rule 70

When parking your cycle:

• find a conspicuous location where passers-by can see it
• use cycle stands or other cycle-parking facilities wherever possible
• do not leave it where it would obstruct or endanger other road users
• secure it properly so that it cannot fall over and become an obstruction or hazard.

Rule 71

At traffic-light junctions and cycle-only crossings with traffic lights, you MUST NOT cross the stop line while the lights are red.

Some junctions have an advanced stop line that allows you to position yourself ahead of other traffic and wait. See Rule 178. When the lights are red, you may cross the first stop line, but you MUST NOT cross the final stop line.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 14, Part 1.

Rule 72

Road positioning

There are two basic road positions cyclists should adopt, depending on the situation.

1. Ride in the centre of your lane to make yourself as clearly visible as possible:

• on quiet roads or streets — if a faster vehicle approaches from behind, move left to allow it to overtake if you can do so safely
• in slower-moving traffic — when traffic begins to flow more freely, move left if it is safe so faster vehicles behind can overtake
• when approaching junctions or road narrowings where it would be unsafe for drivers to overtake.

2. On busy roads where vehicles are moving faster than you, allow them to overtake where it is safe while remaining at least 0.5 metres from the kerb edge, and farther away where this is safer.

Traffic on most dual carriageways moves quickly. Take extra care when crossing slip roads.

category: The Highway Code. 5. Rules for cyclists (59 to 82)
description:
Road junctions (Rules 73 to 77)

Rule 73

Junctions

Some junctions, particularly those with traffic lights, have special cycle facilities. These include small cycle traffic lights at eye-level height, which may allow cyclists to move or cross separately from or ahead of other traffic.

Use these facilities where they make your journey safer and easier.

At junctions without separate cyclist facilities, it is recommended that you proceed as though you were driving a motor vehicle. See Rules 170 to 190.

Position yourself in the centre of your chosen lane where you feel able to do so safely. This will make you as visible as possible and help prevent other vehicles from overtaking where doing so would be dangerous.

If you do not feel safe proceeding in this way, you may prefer to dismount and wheel your cycle across the junction.

Rule 74

Turning

When approaching a junction on the left, watch for vehicles turning in front of you, either out of or into the side road.

If you intend to turn left:

• first check for other cyclists or motorcyclists
• signal your intention
• do not ride on the inside of vehicles that are signalling or slowing down to turn left.

If you intend to turn right:

• check the traffic to make sure it is safe
• signal and move to the centre of the road
• wait for a safe gap in oncoming traffic
• give a final look before completing the turn.

It may be safer to wait on the left until there is a safe gap, or to dismount and push your cycle across the road.

When turning into or out of a side road, you should give way to pedestrians who are crossing or waiting to cross. See Rule H2.

Rule 75

Two-stage turns

At some signal-controlled junctions, signs and markings may instruct cyclists to turn right in two stages.

Stage 1: When the traffic lights turn green, cyclists wishing to turn should travel straight ahead to the position marked on the carriageway by a cycle symbol and turn arrow. They should then stop and wait there.

Stage 2: When the traffic lights on the far side of the junction, now facing the cyclists, turn green, the cyclists should complete the manoeuvre.

Rule 76

Going straight ahead

If you are travelling straight ahead at a junction, you have priority over traffic waiting to turn into or out of a side road unless road signs or markings indicate otherwise. See Rule H3.

Check that you can proceed safely, particularly when approaching junctions on the left alongside stationary or slow-moving traffic. Watch for drivers intending to turn across your path.

Remember that the driver ahead may not be able to see you, so consider your speed and position on the road.

Take great care when deciding whether it is safe to pass stationary or slow-moving lorries and other long vehicles, especially when approaching junctions, because their drivers may not be able to see you.

Remember that long vehicles may need to move to the right before turning left. Their rear wheels may then come very close to the kerb while turning. See Rule 67.

Rule 77

Busy roads

When crossing faster or busy main roads, you may find it safer and easier to:

• dismount and push your cycle across
• wait for a safe gap in traffic before crossing, especially on faster roads and dual carriageways
• use traffic islands or central reservations where appropriate.

category: The Highway Code. 5. Rules for cyclists (59 to 82)
description:
Roundabouts (Rules 78 to 80)

Rule 78

Full details of the correct procedure at roundabouts without cycle facilities are provided in Rules 184 to 190.

Watch for vehicles crossing your path to leave or join the roundabout. Remember that drivers may not easily see you.

Rule 79

Turning right

If you are turning right, you may ride in either the left-hand or right-hand lane and move left as you approach your exit.

Position yourself in the centre of your lane if it is safe to do so. See Rule 72. Signal right to indicate that you are not leaving the roundabout.

Alternatively, you may feel safer dismounting and walking your cycle around the roundabout on the pavement or verge.

If you decide to ride around the roundabout in the left-hand lane, you should:

• be aware that drivers may not easily see you
• take extra care when cycling across exits
• signal right to show that you are not leaving the roundabout
• watch for vehicles crossing your path to leave or join the roundabout.

Where a roundabout has separate cycle facilities, you should use them where they make your journey safer and easier. However, you are not obliged to use them. Whether to use them will depend on your experience, skills and the situation at the time.

Rule 80

Give long vehicles plenty of room on a roundabout because they need more space to manoeuvre.

Do not ride in the space a long vehicle needs to travel around the roundabout. It may be safer to wait until the long vehicle has cleared the roundabout.

category: The Highway Code. 5. Rules for cyclists (59 to 82)
description:
Crossing the road (Rules 81 to 82)

Rule 81

Do not ride across equestrian crossings because they are for horse riders only.

Do not ride across pelican, puffin or zebra crossings. Dismount and wheel your cycle across.

Rule 82

Crossings

Toucan crossings are light-controlled crossings that allow cyclists and pedestrians to share the crossing space and cross at the same time. They are operated by push button.

Pedestrians and cyclists see the green signal together. Cyclists are permitted to ride across.

Cycle tracks on opposite sides of a road may be connected by cycle-only signal-controlled crossings. You may ride across, but you MUST NOT cross until the green cycle symbol is showing.

Cycle-track crossings may be located in spacious pedestrian environments. Cyclists should look out and be prepared to stop for pedestrians crossing the track informally as well as at designated crossing points.

Take extra care when crossing railway level crossings and tramways. See Rule 306.

You should dismount at level crossings where a ‘cyclist dismount’ sign is displayed.

Law: TSRGD Schedule 14, Part 1.

category: The Highway Code. 6. Rules for motorcyclists (83 to 88)
description:
General (Rules 83 to 88)

Rule 83

Protective helmets

On all journeys, the rider and pillion passenger on a motorcycle, scooter or moped MUST wear a protective helmet.

This requirement does not apply to a follower of the Sikh religion while wearing a turban.

Helmets MUST:

• comply with the Regulations
• be fastened securely.

Riders and passengers of motor tricycles and quadricycles, also called quadbikes, should also wear protective helmets.

Before every journey, check that your helmet visor is clean and in good condition.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 16 and 17, and MC(PH)R, as amended, regulation 4.

Rule 84

Protective equipment and clothing

It is advisable to wear eye protectors. If worn, they MUST comply with the Regulations.

Scratched or poorly fitting eye protectors can restrict your view when riding, particularly in bright sunshine and during the hours of darkness.

Consider wearing ear protection. Strong boots, gloves and suitable clothing may help protect you if you are involved in a collision.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 18 and MC(EP)R, as amended, regulation 4.

Rule 85

Pillion passengers

You MUST NOT carry more than one pillion passenger. The passenger MUST sit astride the motorcycle on a proper seat.

The passenger should:

• face forward
• keep both feet on the footrests.

You MUST NOT carry a pillion passenger unless your motorcycle is designed to carry one.

Provisional licence holders MUST NOT carry a pillion passenger.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 23, MV(DL)R regulation 16(6) and CUR regulation 102.

Rule 86

Daylight riding

Make yourself as visible as possible from the sides, front and rear.

You could wear:

• a light-coloured or brightly coloured helmet
• fluorescent clothing or strips.

Using dipped headlights, even in good daylight, may also make you more conspicuous.

However, be aware that other drivers may still not have seen you or may have judged your distance or speed incorrectly, especially at junctions.

Rule 87

Riding in the dark

Wear reflective clothing or strips to improve your visibility in the dark. These reflect light from other vehicles’ headlamps, making you visible from a greater distance.

See Rules 113 to 116 for lighting requirements.

Rule 88

Manoeuvring

Before manoeuvring, be aware of what is behind you and to both sides. Look behind and use your mirrors if they are fitted.

When travelling in traffic queues, watch for:

• pedestrians crossing between vehicles
• vehicles emerging from junctions
• vehicles changing lanes.

Position yourself so that drivers ahead can see you in their mirrors.

When filtering through slow-moving traffic, take care and keep your speed low.

Remember: Observation – Signal – Manoeuvre.

category: The Highway Code. 7. Rules for drivers and motorcyclists (89 to 102)
description:
Rule 89

Vehicle condition

You MUST ensure that your vehicle and trailer comply with the full requirements of:

• the Road Vehicles (Construction and Use) Regulations
• the Road Vehicles Lighting Regulations.

See ‘The road user and the law’.

category: The Highway Code. 7. Rules for drivers and motorcyclists (89 to 102)
description:
Fitness to drive (Rules 90 to 94)

Rule 90

Make sure that you are fit to drive.

You MUST report to the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) any health condition likely to affect your driving.

Law: RTA 1988 section 94.

Rule 91

Tiredness

Driving while tired greatly increases your risk of a collision. To minimise this risk:

• make sure you are fit to drive
• do not begin a journey if you are tired
• get sufficient sleep before starting a long journey
• avoid long journeys between midnight and 6 am, when natural alertness is at its lowest
• plan your journey to include sufficient breaks
• take a minimum break of at least 15 minutes after every two hours of driving
• if you feel sleepy, stop in a safe place.

Do not stop in an emergency area or on the hard shoulder of a motorway to rest. See Rule 262 for guidance on places to take a break when travelling on motorways.

Rule 92

Vision

In good daylight, you MUST be able to read a vehicle number plate from:

• 20 metres for a current-style number plate
• 20.5 metres for an old-style number plate.

If you need glasses or contact lenses to meet this requirement, you MUST wear them at all times while driving.

The police have the power to require a driver to take an eyesight test.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 96, and MV(DL)R regulation 40 and Schedule 8.

Rule 93

Bright sunlight

Slow down and, if necessary, stop if bright sunlight dazzles you.

Rule 94

Tinted glasses, lenses and visors

At night or in poor visibility, do not use tinted glasses, lenses or visors if they restrict your vision.

category: The Highway Code. 7. Rules for drivers and motorcyclists (89 to 102)
description:
Alcohol and drugs (Rules 95 to 96)

Rule 95

Alcohol

Do not drink and drive because alcohol will seriously affect your judgement and abilities.

In England and Wales, you MUST NOT drive with:

• a breath alcohol level higher than 35 microgrammes per 100 millilitres of breath
• a blood alcohol level of more than 80 milligrammes per 100 millilitres of blood.

In Scotland, the legal limits are lower. You MUST NOT drive with:

• a breath alcohol level higher than 22 microgrammes per 100 millilitres of breath
• a blood alcohol level of more than 50 milligrammes per 100 millilitres of blood.

Alcohol will:

• give you a false sense of confidence
• reduce coordination and slow your reactions
• affect your judgement of speed, distance and risk
• reduce your driving ability, even if you are below the legal limit
• take time to leave your body.

You may be unfit to drive in the evening after drinking at lunchtime or in the morning after drinking the previous evening.

The best solution is not to drink at all when planning to drive because any amount of alcohol affects your ability to drive safely. If you are going to drink, arrange another means of transport.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 4, 5 and 11(2), and PLSR.

Rule 96

Drugs and medicines

You MUST NOT drive under the influence of drugs or medicine.

For medicines, check with your doctor or pharmacist. Do not drive if you are advised that the medicine may impair you.

You MUST NOT drive if you have illegal drugs or certain medicines in your blood above the specified limits.

Taking illegal drugs before driving is highly dangerous. Never take illegal drugs if you intend to drive. Their effects are unpredictable, can be even more severe than those of alcohol and can result in fatal or serious road crashes.

Illegal drugs have been assigned very low specified limits, so even small amounts may put you above those limits.

The specified limits for certain medicines are higher than the levels generally found in the blood of patients who have taken normal therapeutic doses.

If a drug concentration in your blood is above its specified limit because you were prescribed or legitimately supplied a particularly high dose of medicine, you may raise a statutory medical defence, provided that your driving was not impaired by the medicine you were taking.

Law: RTA 1988 sections 4 and 5.

category: The Highway Code. 7. Rules for drivers and motorcyclists (89 to 102)
description:
Rule 97

Before setting off

You MUST ensure that:

• you have a valid licence and insurance to drive the vehicle you intend to use — see ‘Motor vehicle documentation and learner driver requirements’
• your vehicle is legal and roadworthy — see ‘Motor vehicle documentation and learner driver requirements’ and ‘Vehicle maintenance, safety and security’ for important vehicle maintenance and safety checks.

You SHOULD ensure that:

• you have planned your route and allowed sufficient time for breaks and possible delays
• you have sufficient fuel or charge for your journey, especially if it includes motorway driving
• you know where all the controls are and how to use them
• your clothing and footwear do not prevent you from using the controls correctly
• your mirrors and seat are adjusted correctly to provide comfort, full control and maximum vision
• your head restraints are adjusted correctly to reduce the risk of neck and spinal injuries in a collision.

For emergency use, it is recommended that:

• you have a mobile telephone containing emergency contacts, such as breakdown assistance
• you have high-visibility clothing.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 42, 45, 47, 49, 53, 87, 99(4) and 143; MV(DL)R regulations 16 and 40 and Schedule 4; VERA section 29; RVLR 1989 regulations 23 and 27; and CUR regulations 27, 30, 32 and 61.

category: The Highway Code. 7. Rules for drivers and motorcyclists (89 to 102)
description:
Rule 98

Vehicle towing and loading

Before towing

As a driver:

• you MUST NOT tow more than your licence permits. If you passed your car driving test on or after 1 January 1997, restrictions apply to the weight of trailer you may tow
• you MUST ensure that your vehicle and trailer are roadworthy. This includes checking that all tyres are legal, the trailer braking system is fully operational and all trailer lights work correctly
• you MUST NOT overload your vehicle or trailer
• you should not tow a weight greater than the vehicle manufacturer recommends
• you should distribute the weight in your caravan or trailer evenly, with heavy items over the axle or axles, and ensure a downward load on the tow ball
• you should not exceed the manufacturer’s recommended weight or tow-ball load. Correct weight distribution should minimise the possibility of swerving, snaking and losing control
• you MUST secure your load, and it MUST NOT project dangerously
• you must ensure that heavy or sharp objects and animals are secured safely. In a collision, unsecured objects or animals could strike someone inside the vehicle and cause serious injury
• towing mirrors MUST be used if your vehicle is narrower than your trailer or load, or if the trailer or load obstructs your rearward view
• your trailer MUST have a secondary coupling device, such as a safety chain
• carrying a load or towing a trailer may require you to adjust your headlights.

During towing

As a driver:

• be aware that reduced speed limits apply — see Rule 124
• be aware that your stopping distance may increase significantly — see Rule 126
• you MUST NOT use the right-hand lane of a motorway with three or more lanes — see Rule 265
• if the trailer begins to swerve or snake, or you lose control, ease off the accelerator and reduce speed gently to regain control. Do not brake harshly.

Breakdowns

If a breakdown occurs, remember that:

• towing a vehicle with a tow rope is potentially dangerous; consider using a solid tow bar or professional recovery instead
• it may take longer to build up speed when rejoining a carriageway — see also Rule 278.

For additional advice about towing safely, see Further reading.

Laws: CUR regulations 27, 33, 86A and 100; RVLR regulation 18; MT(E&W)R regulation 12; and MV(DL)R regulations 6, 7 and 76 and Schedule 2.

category: The Highway Code. 7. Rules for drivers and motorcyclists (89 to 102)
subcategory: Seat belts and child restraints (rules 99 to 102)
englishSubcategory: Seat belts and child restraints (rules 99 to 102)
description:
Seat belts and child restraints (Rules 99 to 102)

Rule 99

You MUST wear a seat belt in cars, vans and other goods vehicles if one is fitted.

Adults and children aged 14 years or older MUST use a seat belt or child restraint, where fitted, when seated in minibuses, buses and coaches.

Exemptions are allowed for:

• holders of medical exemption certificates
• people making deliveries or collections in goods vehicles when travelling less than 50 metres, approximately 162 feet.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 14 and 15; MV(WSB)R; MV(WSBCFS)R; and MV(WSB)(A)R 2005 and 2006.

Seat-belt requirements

The following summarises the main legal requirements for wearing seat belts in cars, vans and other goods vehicles.

Driver

• Front seat: a seat belt MUST be worn if fitted.
• Responsibility: the driver.

Child under 3 years old

• Front seat: the correct child restraint MUST be used.
• Rear seat: the correct child restraint MUST be used. If one is unavailable in a taxi, the child may travel unrestrained.
• Responsibility: the driver.

Child from their third birthday until reaching 1.35 metres in height or their 12th birthday, whichever occurs first

• Front seat: the correct child restraint MUST be used.
• Rear seat: the correct child restraint MUST be used where seat belts are fitted.
• An adult seat belt MUST be used if the correct child restraint is unavailable in a licensed taxi or private-hire vehicle, for reasons of unexpected necessity over a short distance, or because two occupied restraints prevent a third restraint from being fitted.
• Responsibility: the driver.

Child taller than 1.35 metres, approximately 4 feet 5 inches, or aged 12 or 13

• Front seat: a seat belt MUST be worn if available.
• Rear seat: a seat belt MUST be worn if available.
• Responsibility: the driver.

Adult passengers aged 14 or older

• Front seat: a seat belt MUST be worn if available.
• Rear seat: a seat belt MUST be worn if available.
• Responsibility: the passenger.

Rule 100

The driver MUST ensure that every child under 14 years old in a car, van or other goods vehicle wears a seat belt or uses an approved child restraint where required.

If a child is under 1.35 metres, approximately 4 feet 5 inches, a baby seat, child seat, booster seat or booster cushion MUST be used. It must be suitable for the child’s weight and fitted according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 14 and 15; MV(WSB)R; MV(WSBCFS)R; and MV(WSB)(A)R 2006.

Rule 101

A rear-facing baby seat MUST NOT be fitted to a seat protected by an active frontal airbag. In a collision, the airbag could cause serious injury or death to the child.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 14 and 15; MV(WSB)R; MV(WSBCFS)R; and MV(WSB)(A)R 2006.

Rule 102

Children in cars, vans and other goods vehicles

Drivers carrying children should also ensure that:

• children enter the vehicle through the door nearest the kerb
• child restraints are fitted correctly according to the manufacturer’s instructions
• children do not sit behind the rear seats in an estate car or hatchback unless a special child seat has been fitted
• child-safety door locks are used, where fitted, when children are in the vehicle
• children are kept under control.

category: The Highway Code. 8. General rules, techniques and advice for all drivers and riders (103 to 158)
description:
Signals (Rules 103 to 106)

Rule 103

Signals warn and inform other road users, including pedestrians, of your intended actions. See ‘Signals to other road users’.

You should always:

• give clear signals in plenty of time, after checking that signalling at that time will not be misleading
• use signals to advise other road users before changing course or direction, stopping or moving off
• cancel signals after use
• make sure your signals will not confuse others
• use an arm signal to emphasise or reinforce your signal if necessary.

For example, if you intend to stop after a side road, do not signal until you are passing the road. Signalling earlier may give the impression that you intend to turn into it. Your brake lights will warn traffic behind that you are slowing down.

Remember that signalling does not give you priority.

Rule 104

You should also:

• watch for signals given by other road users and proceed only when you are satisfied that it is safe
• remember that an indicator on another vehicle may not have been cancelled.

Rule 105

You MUST obey signals given by:

• police officers
• traffic officers
• traffic wardens — see ‘Signals by authorised persons’
• signs used by school crossing patrols.

Laws: RTRA section 28; RTA 1988 section 35; TMA section 6; and FTWO article 3.

Rule 106

Police stopping procedures

If the police want you to stop your vehicle, they will, where possible, attract your attention by:

• flashing blue lights or headlights, or sounding a siren or horn, usually from behind
• directing you to pull over by pointing and/or using the left indicator.

You MUST then pull over and stop as soon as it is safe to do so. After stopping, switch off your engine.

Law: RTA 1988 section 163.

category: The Highway Code. 8. General rules, techniques and advice for all drivers and riders (103 to 158)
description:
Other stopping procedures (Rules 107 to 112)

Rule 107

Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency officers

Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency officers have the power to stop vehicles on all roads, including motorways and trunk roads.

They will attract your attention by flashing amber lights:

• from the front, requesting that you follow them to a safe place to stop
• from behind, directing you to pull over by pointing and/or using the left indicator.

It is an offence not to comply with their directions. You MUST obey any signals they give. See ‘Signals by authorised persons’.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 67, and PRA section 41 and Schedule 5(8).

Rule 108

Traffic officers

Traffic officers have powers to stop vehicles on most motorways and some ‘A’ roads in England and Wales.

If uniformed traffic officers want to stop your vehicle on safety grounds, such as an insecure load, they will, where possible, attract your attention by:

• flashing amber lights, usually from behind
• directing you to pull over by pointing and/or using the left indicator.

You MUST then pull over and stop as soon as it is safe. After stopping, switch off your engine.

It is an offence not to comply with their directions. See ‘Signals by authorised persons’.

Law: RTA 1988 sections 35 and 163, as amended by TMA section 6.

Rule 109

Traffic-light signals and traffic signs

You MUST obey:

• all traffic-light signals — see ‘Light signals controlling traffic’
• all traffic signs giving orders, including temporary signals and signs — see ‘Traffic signs’.

Make sure you know, understand and act on all other traffic and information signs and road markings. See ‘Traffic signs’, ‘Road markings’ and ‘Vehicle markings’.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 3, Part 4; Schedule 9, Parts 7 and 8; Schedule 14, Parts 1 and 5; Schedule 7, Part 6; and Schedule 15, Part 1.

Rule 110

Flashing headlights

Flash your headlights only to let other road users know that you are there.

Do not flash your headlights to communicate any other message or intimidate other road users.

Rule 111

Never assume that flashing headlights are an invitation to proceed. Use your own judgement and proceed carefully.

Rule 112

The horn

Use your horn only while your vehicle is moving and when you need to warn other road users of your presence.

Never sound your horn aggressively.

You MUST NOT use your horn:

• while stationary on the road
• when driving in a built-up area between 11:30 pm and 7:00 am
• except when another road user poses a danger.

Law: CUR regulation 99.

category: The Highway Code. 8. General rules, techniques and advice for all drivers and riders (103 to 158)
description:
Lighting requirements (Rules 113 to 116)

Rule 113

You MUST:

• ensure that all sidelights and rear registration-plate lights are lit between sunset and sunrise
• use headlights at night, except on a road with lit street lighting. Such roads are generally restricted to 30 mph (48 km/h), or 20 mph (32 km/h) in Wales, unless otherwise specified
• use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced — see Rule 226.

Night, meaning the hours of darkness, is defined as the period from half an hour after sunset until half an hour before sunrise.

Laws: RVLR regulations 3, 24 and 25; in Scotland, RTRA section 82, as amended by NRSWA, paragraph 59 of Schedule 8; and RR(20)O.

Rule 114

You MUST NOT:

• use any lights in a way that dazzles or causes discomfort to other road users, including pedestrians, cyclists and horse riders
• use front or rear fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced.

You MUST switch off your fog lights when visibility improves to avoid dazzling other road users. See Rule 226.

In stationary traffic queues, drivers should apply the parking brake. Once following traffic has stopped, take your foot off the footbrake to deactivate the brake lights. This will minimise glare for road users behind until traffic begins moving again.

Law: RVLR regulation 27.

Rule 115

You should also:

• use dipped headlights, or dim-dip lights if fitted, at night in built-up areas and during dull daytime weather so that you can be seen
• keep your headlights dipped while overtaking until you are level with the other vehicle, and then use the main beam if necessary, unless doing so would dazzle oncoming road users
• slow down and, if necessary, stop if dazzled by oncoming headlights.

Rule 116

Hazard warning lights

Hazard warning lights may be used while your vehicle is stationary to warn that it is temporarily obstructing traffic. Never use them as an excuse for dangerous or illegal parking.

You MUST NOT use hazard warning lights while driving or being towed unless:

• you are on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway
• you need to warn drivers behind you of a hazard or obstruction ahead.

Use hazard warning lights only for long enough to ensure that your warning has been observed.

Law: RVLR regulation 27.

category: The Highway Code. 8. General rules, techniques and advice for all drivers and riders (103 to 158)
description:
Control of the vehicle (Rules 117 to 126)

Braking

Rule 117

In normal circumstances

The safest way to brake is to brake early and lightly. Brake more firmly as you begin to stop. Ease the pressure just before the vehicle comes to rest to avoid a jerky stop.

Rule 118

In an emergency

Brake immediately. Try not to brake so harshly that the wheels lock, as locked wheels can cause loss of control.

Rule 119

Skids

Skidding is usually caused by:

• braking too harshly
• accelerating too harshly
• steering too harshly
• driving too fast for the road conditions.

If a skid occurs, remove its cause by releasing the brake pedal fully or easing off the accelerator. Turn the steering wheel in the direction of the skid. For example, if the rear of the vehicle skids to the right, steer immediately to the right to recover.

Rule 120

Anti-lock braking systems (ABS)

If your vehicle has anti-lock brakes, follow the advice in its handbook.

In an emergency, apply the footbrake firmly and do not release the pressure until the vehicle has slowed to the desired speed. ABS should allow you to retain steering control, but do not assume that a vehicle with ABS will stop in a shorter distance.

Rule 121

Brakes affected by water

After driving through deep water, your brakes may be less effective. Test them at the first safe opportunity by pressing the brake pedal gently.

If the brakes are not fully effective, apply light pressure gently while driving slowly. This will help dry them.

Rule 122

Coasting

Coasting means travelling in neutral or with the clutch pressed down. It can reduce driver control because:

• engine braking is eliminated
• speed will increase quickly downhill
• increased use of the footbrake can reduce its effectiveness
• steering response is affected, particularly on bends and corners
• selecting the appropriate gear when needed may be more difficult.

Rule 123

The driver and the environment

You MUST NOT:

• leave a parked vehicle unattended with its engine running
• leave an engine running unnecessarily while the vehicle is stationary on a public road.

Generally, if a vehicle is stationary and likely to remain so for more than a couple of minutes, apply the parking brake and switch off the engine to reduce emissions and noise pollution.

The engine may remain running if the vehicle is stationary in traffic or if it is being used to diagnose faults.

Law: CUR regulations 98 and 107.

Rule 124

Speed limits

You MUST NOT exceed the maximum speed limit for the road or your vehicle.

Unless signs indicate otherwise, roads with street lights, excluding motorways, generally have a speed limit of:

• 30 mph (48 km/h) in England and Scotland
• 20 mph (32 km/h) in Wales.

Maximum speed limits

Cars and motorcycles, including car-derived vans up to 2 tonnes maximum laden weight:

• built-up areas in England and Scotland: 30 mph (48 km/h)
• built-up areas in Wales: 20 mph (32 km/h)
• single carriageways: 60 mph (96 km/h)
• dual carriageways: 70 mph (112 km/h)
• motorways: 70 mph (112 km/h).

Cars towing caravans or trailers, including car-derived vans and motorcycles:

• built-up areas in England and Scotland: 30 mph (48 km/h)
• built-up areas in Wales: 20 mph (32 km/h)
• single carriageways: 50 mph (80 km/h)
• dual carriageways: 60 mph (96 km/h)
• motorways: 60 mph (96 km/h).

Motorhomes or motor caravans not exceeding 3.05 tonnes maximum unladen weight:

• built-up areas in England and Scotland: 30 mph (48 km/h)
• built-up areas in Wales: 20 mph (32 km/h)
• single carriageways: 60 mph (96 km/h)
• dual carriageways: 70 mph (112 km/h)
• motorways: 70 mph (112 km/h).

Motorhomes or motor caravans exceeding 3.05 tonnes maximum unladen weight:

• built-up areas in England and Scotland: 30 mph (48 km/h)
• built-up areas in Wales: 20 mph (32 km/h)
• single carriageways: 50 mph (80 km/h)
• dual carriageways: 60 mph (96 km/h)
• motorways: 70 mph (112 km/h).

Buses, coaches and minibuses not exceeding 12 metres in overall length:

• built-up areas in England and Scotland: 30 mph (48 km/h)
• built-up areas in Wales: 20 mph (32 km/h)
• single carriageways: 50 mph (80 km/h)
• dual carriageways: 60 mph (96 km/h)
• motorways: 70 mph (112 km/h).

The motorway limit is 60 mph (96 km/h) if the vehicle exceeds 12 metres in overall length.

Goods vehicles not exceeding 7.5 tonnes maximum laden weight:

• built-up areas in England and Scotland: 30 mph (48 km/h)
• built-up areas in Wales: 20 mph (32 km/h)
• single carriageways: 50 mph (80 km/h)
• dual carriageways: 60 mph (96 km/h)
• motorways: 70 mph (112 km/h).

The motorway limit is 60 mph (96 km/h) if the goods vehicle is articulated or towing a trailer.

Goods vehicles exceeding 7.5 tonnes maximum laden weight in England and Wales:

• built-up areas in England and Scotland: 30 mph (48 km/h)
• built-up areas in Wales: 20 mph (32 km/h)
• single carriageways: 50 mph (80 km/h)
• dual carriageways: 60 mph (96 km/h)
• motorways: 60 mph (96 km/h).

Goods vehicles exceeding 7.5 tonnes maximum laden weight in Scotland:

• built-up areas in England and Scotland: 30 mph (48 km/h)
• built-up areas in Wales: 20 mph (32 km/h)
• single carriageways: 40 mph (64 km/h)
• dual carriageways: 50 mph (80 km/h)
• motorways: 60 mph (96 km/h).

For limits applying to special vehicle types, including oversized vehicles, see Further reading.

Locally set limits may include:

• 20 mph (32 km/h) in some built-up areas in England and Scotland
• 30 mph (48 km/h) in some built-up areas in Wales
• 50 mph (80 km/h) on single carriageways with known hazards
• variable maximum speed limits on some motorways and dual carriageways.

Speed limits are enforced by the police.

Law: RTRA sections 81, 86 and 89 and Schedule 6, as amended by MV(VSL)(E&W), and RR(20)O.

Rule 125

Safe speed

The speed limit is the absolute maximum. It does not mean that driving at that speed is safe in all conditions.

Unsafe speed increases the likelihood of causing or being unable to avoid a collision, as well as the collision’s severity. Inappropriate speeds also intimidate people and discourage walking, cycling and horse riding.

Driving too fast for the road and traffic conditions is dangerous. Always reduce your speed when:

• the road layout or condition presents hazards, such as bends
• sharing the road with pedestrians, particularly children, older adults or disabled people, cyclists, horse riders, horse-drawn vehicles and motorcyclists
• weather conditions make a lower speed safer
• driving at night, when other road users are more difficult to see.

Stopping distances

Drive at a speed that allows you to stop well within the distance you can see to be clear.

You should:

• leave enough space to stop safely if the vehicle ahead suddenly slows or stops; never get closer than the overall stopping distance
• allow at least a two-second gap on high-speed roads and in tunnels where visibility is reduced
• at least double this gap on wet roads
• increase it by up to ten times on icy roads
• remember that large vehicles and motorcycles need a greater stopping distance
• allow a four-second gap when driving a large vehicle in a tunnel
• leave at least a 5-metre gap from the vehicle ahead if you have to stop in a tunnel.

Tailgating occurs when the gap to the vehicle ahead is too small for you to stop safely if that vehicle brakes suddenly.

Tailgating is dangerous and intimidating and can cause collisions, especially at speed. A safe following distance gives you time to react and stop if necessary.

Dangerous and careless driving offences, including tailgating, are enforced by the police.

category: The Highway Code. 8. General rules, techniques and advice for all drivers and riders (103 to 158)
subcategory: Lines and lane markings on the road (rules 127 to 132)
englishSubcategory: Lines and lane markings on the road (rules 127 to 132)
description:
Lines and lane markings on the road (Rules 127 to 132)

Rule 127

Broken white lines

A broken white line marks the centre of the road.

When the lines become longer and the gaps become shorter, there is a hazard ahead.

Do not cross the line unless you can see that the road is clear and you intend to overtake or turn off.

Rule 128

Double white lines with the line nearer to you broken

You may cross the lines to overtake if it is safe, provided that you can complete the manoeuvre before reaching a solid white line on your side.

White direction arrows on the road indicate that you need to return to your side of the road.

Rule 129

Double white lines with the line nearer to you solid

You MUST NOT cross or straddle the solid line unless it is safe and you need to enter adjoining premises or a side road.

If necessary and provided the road is clear, you may cross the line to:

• pass a stationary vehicle
• overtake a pedal cycle travelling at 10 mph (16 km/h) or less
• overtake a horse travelling at 10 mph (16 km/h) or less
• overtake a road-maintenance vehicle travelling at 10 mph (16 km/h) or less.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 9, Part 8.

Rule 130

Areas of white diagonal stripes or chevrons

These areas separate traffic lanes or protect traffic turning right.

If the area is bordered by a broken white line, you should not enter it unless entry is necessary and you can see that it is safe.

If the area has chevrons and is bordered by solid white lines, you MUST NOT enter it except in an emergency.

Laws: MT(E&W)R regulations 5, 9, 10 and 16; MT(S)R regulations 4, 8, 9 and 14; RTA 1988 section 36; and TSRGD Schedule 9, Part 8.

Rule 131

Lane dividers

Lane dividers are short, broken white lines used on wide carriageways to divide them into lanes. You should keep between them.

Rule 132

Reflective road studs

Reflective road studs may be used with white lines.

• White studs mark lanes or the middle of the road.
• Red studs mark the left edge of the road.
• Amber studs mark the central reservation of a dual carriageway or motorway.
• Green studs mark the edge of the main carriageway at lay-bys and slip roads.
• Green and yellow studs indicate temporary changes to lane layouts, for example where roadworks are taking place.

category: The Highway Code. 8. General rules, techniques and advice for all drivers and riders (103 to 158)
description:
Multi-lane carriageways (Rules 133 to 143)

Lane discipline

Rule 133

Before changing lanes:

• use your mirrors
• if necessary, take a quick sideways glance
• make sure you will not force another road user to change course or speed
• when it is safe, signal your intentions to other road users
• move over when the way is clear.

Rule 134

Follow signs and road markings and enter the lane as directed.
