In congested conditions, do not change lanes unnecessarily.

Merging in turn is recommended only when it is safe and appropriate and vehicles are moving at a very low speed, such as when approaching roadworks or a road traffic incident. It is not recommended at high speed.

Single carriageways

Rule 135

On a three-lane single carriageway where signs or markings do not give priority to traffic in either direction:

• use the middle lane only for overtaking or turning right
• remember that you have no more right to use the middle lane than a driver approaching from the opposite direction
• do not use the right-hand lane.

Rule 136

Where a single carriageway has four or more lanes, use only the lanes indicated by signs or road markings.

Dual carriageways

A dual carriageway is a road with a central reservation separating its carriageways.

Rule 137

On a two-lane dual carriageway, stay in the left-hand lane. Use the right-hand lane for overtaking or turning right.

After overtaking, return to the left-hand lane when it is safe.

Rule 138

On a dual carriageway with three or more lanes, you may use the middle or right-hand lanes to overtake. Return to the middle lanes and then to the left-hand lane when it is safe.

Rule 139

Climbing and crawler lanes

Climbing and crawler lanes are provided on some hills.

Use one if:

• you are driving a slow-moving vehicle
• vehicles behind you wish to overtake.

Watch for signs and road markings indicating that the lane is about to end.

Rule 140

Cycle lanes and cycle tracks

Cycle lanes are indicated by road markings and signs.

You MUST NOT drive or park in a cycle lane marked by a solid white line during its hours of operation.

Do not drive or park in a cycle lane marked by a broken white line unless this is unavoidable.

You MUST NOT park in any cycle lane while waiting restrictions apply.

Give way to cyclists in a cycle lane, including cyclists approaching from behind. Do not cut across them when turning or changing lanes. See Rule H3.

Be prepared to stop and wait for a safe gap in the flow of cyclists before crossing a cycle lane.

Cycle tracks are routes for cyclists that are physically protected from or located away from motor traffic, except where they cross side roads. Cycle tracks may be shared with pedestrians.

When turning into or out of a junction, give way to cyclists approaching or using a cycle track. See Rule H3.

Be prepared to stop and wait for a safe gap before crossing a cycle track. Remember that cyclists may use the track in both directions.

Cyclists are not obliged to use cycle lanes or cycle tracks.

Law: RTRA sections 5 and 8.

Rule 141

Bus lanes

Bus lanes are identified by road markings and signs. The signs indicate which other vehicles, if any, may use the lane.

Unless signs indicate otherwise, do not drive in a bus lane during its operating period.

You may enter a bus lane to stop, load or unload where this is not prohibited.

Rule 142

High-occupancy vehicle lanes and other designated vehicle lanes

Some lanes are restricted to particular types of vehicle. Restrictions may apply for some or all of the time. Traffic signs show the operating times and permitted vehicle types.

You MUST NOT drive in a designated lane during its operating period unless signs indicate that your vehicle is permitted. See ‘Traffic signs’.

Vehicles permitted to use designated lanes may or may not include:

• cycles
• buses
• taxis
• licensed private-hire vehicles
• motorcycles
• heavy goods vehicles (HGVs)
• high-occupancy vehicles (HOVs).

While an HOV lane is operating, it MUST ONLY be used by:

• vehicles containing at least the minimum number of people shown on the traffic signs
• other vehicles, such as buses and motorcycles, where signs before the start of the lane permit them, regardless of their number of occupants.

Laws: RTRA sections 5 and 8, and RTA 1988 section 36.

Rule 143

One-way streets

Traffic MUST travel in the direction indicated by signs. Buses and/or cycles may have a contraflow lane.

Choose the correct lane for your exit as soon as possible. Do not change lanes suddenly.

Unless signs or road markings indicate otherwise, use:

• the left-hand lane when turning left
• the right-hand lane when turning right
• the most appropriate lane when travelling straight ahead.

Remember that traffic may pass on both sides.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and RTRA sections 5 and 8.

category: The Highway Code. 8. General rules, techniques and advice for all drivers and riders (103 to 158)
description:
General advice (Rules 144 to 158)

Rule 144

You MUST NOT:

• drive dangerously
• drive without due care and attention
• drive without reasonable consideration for other road users.

Driving requires focus and attention at all times. You may be driving dangerously or travelling too fast even if you do not intend to.

Law: RTA 1988 sections 2 and 3, as amended by RTA 1991.

Rule 145

You MUST NOT drive on or over a pavement, footpath or bridleway except to gain lawful access to property or in an emergency.

Laws: HA 1835 section 72 and RTA 1988 section 34.

Rule 146

Adapt your driving to the type and condition of the road. In particular:

• do not treat speed limits as targets; driving at the maximum limit is often inappropriate or unsafe
• consider the road and traffic conditions
• be prepared for unexpected or difficult situations, such as a blocked road beyond a blind bend
• adjust your speed as a precaution
• be prepared for road users emerging at junctions
• on side roads and country lanes, watch for unmarked junctions where nobody has priority
• be prepared to stop at traffic-control systems, roadworks, pedestrian crossings or traffic lights
• anticipate what pedestrians and cyclists may do
• remember that pedestrians, particularly children, may step into the road without seeing you if they are looking the other way.

Rule 147

Be considerate

Be careful of and considerate towards every type of road user, especially those requiring extra care. See Rule 204.

You MUST NOT throw anything from a vehicle, including food, food packaging, cigarette ends, cans, paper or carrier bags. These items can endanger other road users, particularly motorcyclists and cyclists.

Try to be understanding if another road user causes problems, as they may be inexperienced or unfamiliar with the area. Be patient and remember that anyone can make a mistake.

Do not become agitated or involved when someone behaves badly on the road, as this will make the situation worse. Pull over, calm down and continue only when you feel relaxed.

If a road user pulls out into your path at a junction, slow down and hold back to let them clear. Do not overreact by following too closely to intimidate them.

Law: EPA section 87.

Rule 148

Concentration

Safe driving and riding require concentration. Avoid distractions such as:

• loud music, which may mask other sounds
• trying to read maps
• starting or adjusting music or a radio
• arguing with passengers or other road users
• eating and drinking
• smoking.

You MUST NOT smoke in public-transport vehicles or in vehicles used for work in certain prescribed circumstances. Separate regulations apply in England, Wales and Scotland.

In England and Wales, a driver MUST NOT smoke or allow anyone to smoke in an enclosed private vehicle carrying a person under 18. This includes motor caravans.

In Scotland, it is an offence for anyone aged 18 or older to smoke in a private motor vehicle when a person under 18 is present and the vehicle is in a public place. The exception is when the vehicle is parked and being used as living accommodation.

Laws: TSf(EV)R; TSfP(W)R; TPSCP(S)R; S-f(PV)R; S-f(W)R; and SP(CIMV)(S)A.

Mobile phones and in-vehicle technology

Rule 149

You MUST exercise proper control of your vehicle at all times.

You MUST NOT use a hand-held mobile phone or similar device capable of interactive communication, such as a tablet, for any purpose while driving or supervising a learner driver.

The prohibition covers all use of a hand-held interactive communication device, even when its interactive communication capability is switched off or unavailable.

You MUST NOT:

• pick up a phone or similar device while driving to dial a number and then place it in a cradle for the conversation
• pick up and use a hand-held phone or similar device while stationary in traffic.

You may call 999 or 112 in a genuine emergency when stopping is unsafe or impractical.

You may use a hand-held phone or similar device to make a contactless payment at a contactless payment terminal if:

• your vehicle is stationary
• the goods or services are received at the same time as, or after, the payment.

Never use a hand-held microphone while driving.

Hands-free equipment can also distract you. It is much safer not to use a telephone or similar device while driving or riding. Stop in a safe place first, or use voicemail and listen to messages later.

You may park using a hand-held remote-control application or device. The application or device MUST be legal, and you should not endanger anyone while using it.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 2 and 3, and CUR regulations 104 and 110.

Rule 150

In-vehicle systems

Systems such as satellite navigation, congestion warnings, computers and multimedia systems can distract drivers.

You MUST exercise proper control of your vehicle at all times.

Do not rely on driver-assistance systems such as motorway assist, lane-departure warnings or remote-control parking. They provide assistance, but you must not reduce your concentration.

Do not become distracted by maps or screen-based navigation or vehicle-management information while driving or riding. Stop in a safe place if necessary.

You remain responsible for the vehicle while using a driver-assistance system, including motorway assist, or a hand-held remote-control parking application or device. You MUST retain full control over these systems at all times.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 2 and 3, and CUR regulations 104 and 110.

Rule 151

Slow-moving traffic

You should:

• reduce the distance between your vehicle and the vehicle ahead to maintain traffic flow
• never follow so closely that you cannot stop safely
• leave enough space to manoeuvre if the vehicle ahead breaks down or an emergency vehicle needs to pass
• not change to a lane on the left to overtake
• allow access into and from side roads, because blocking them adds to congestion
• allow pedestrians and cyclists to cross in front of you
• watch for cyclists and motorcyclists passing on either side.

Driving in built-up areas

Rule 152

Residential streets

Drive slowly and carefully on streets where pedestrians, cyclists and parked vehicles are likely. A maximum speed limit of 20 mph (32 km/h) may apply in some areas.

Watch for:

• vehicles emerging from junctions or driveways
• vehicles moving off
• opening car doors
• pedestrians
• children running from between parked cars
• cyclists and motorcyclists.

Rule 153

Traffic-calming measures

Some roads have road humps, chicanes and narrowings intended to reduce traffic speed.

When approaching these features:

• reduce your speed
• allow cyclists and motorcyclists room to pass through
• maintain a reduced speed throughout the section covered by the traffic-calming measures
• give way to oncoming road users when signs direct you to do so
• do not overtake moving road users within these areas.

Country roads

Rule 154

Take extra care on country roads. Reduce your speed when approaching:

• bends, which may be sharper than they appear
• junctions and turnings, which may be partly hidden
• villages.

Be prepared for pedestrians, horse riders, cyclists, slow-moving farm vehicles and mud on the road. Make sure you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear.

Rule 155

Single-track roads

Single-track roads are wide enough for only one vehicle and may have special passing places.

If a vehicle approaches you, or a driver behind wants to overtake:

• pull into a passing place on your left
• wait opposite a passing place on your right.

Give way to road users travelling uphill whenever possible. If necessary, reverse to a passing place to let another vehicle pass.

Slow down when passing pedestrians, cyclists and horse riders.

Rule 156

Do not park in passing places.

Vehicles prohibited from using roads and pavements

Rule 157

Certain motorised vehicles do not meet the construction and technical requirements for road vehicles. They are generally not intended, suitable or legal for use on roads, pavements, footpaths, cycle paths or bridleways.

These include most miniature motorcycles, also called mini motos, and motorised scooters, also called go-peds, powered by electric or internal-combustion engines.

These vehicles MUST NOT be used on roads, pavements, footpaths or bridleways.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 34, 41A, 42, 47, 63 and 66; HA 1835 section 72; and R(S)A section 129.

Rule 158

Certain motorcycles, motor tricycles and quadricycles, also called quad bikes, are intended only for off-road use and do not meet the legal standards for road use.

Vehicles that do not meet these standards MUST NOT be used on roads, pavements, footpaths, cycle paths or bridleways.

Before using any motorcycle, motor tricycle, quadricycle or other motor vehicle on a road, you MUST ensure that it:

• meets the legal standards
• is properly registered
• is taxed
• is insured.

Even if a vehicle is registered, taxed and insured for road use, it MUST NOT be used on pavements.

Laws: RTA 1988 sections 34, 41A, 42, 47, 63, 66 and 156; HA 1835 section 72; R(S)A section 129; and VERA sections 1, 29, 31A and 43A.

category: The Highway Code. 9. Using the road (159 to 203)
description:
General rules (Rules 159 to 161)

Rule 159

Before moving off, you should:

• use all mirrors to check that the road is clear
• look around to check your blind spots, which are the areas you cannot see in the mirrors
• signal if necessary before moving out
• look around for a final check.

Move off only when it is safe.

Rule 160

Once moving, you should:

• keep to the left unless road signs or markings indicate otherwise. Exceptions apply when overtaking, turning right, or passing parked vehicles or pedestrians in the road
• keep well to the left on right-hand bends. This improves your view of the road and helps prevent collisions with traffic approaching from the opposite direction
• drive or ride with both hands on the steering wheel or handlebars where possible, helping you retain full control at all times
• use driver-assistance systems only according to the manufacturer’s instructions
• remain aware of other road users, especially cyclists and motorcyclists filtering through traffic. They are harder to see than larger vehicles, and their riders are particularly vulnerable
• give cyclists and motorcyclists plenty of room, especially when driving a long vehicle or towing a trailer
• give way to cyclists when changing direction or lane and do not cut across them
• select a lower gear before reaching a long downhill slope to help control your speed
• remember when towing that the additional length affects overtaking and manoeuvring, while the additional weight affects braking and acceleration.

Rule 161

Mirrors

Use all mirrors effectively throughout your journey. You should:

• use your mirrors frequently so that you always know what is behind you and to each side
• use them in good time before signalling or changing direction or speed
• remember that mirrors do not show every area and that blind spots remain
• look around and check blind spots when necessary.

Remember: Mirrors – Signal – Manoeuvre.

category: The Highway Code. 9. Using the road (159 to 203)
description:
Overtaking (Rules 162 to 169)

Rule 162

Before overtaking, make sure that:

• the road ahead is sufficiently clear
• other road users are not beginning to overtake you
• there is a suitable gap in front of the road user you intend to overtake.

Rule 163

Overtake only when it is safe and legal. You should:

• not get too close to the vehicle you intend to overtake
• use your mirrors, signal when safe, take a quick sideways glance into the blind spot if necessary and then begin moving out
• not assume that you can follow a vehicle ahead that is overtaking, as there may be room for only one vehicle
• once you begin overtaking, move quickly past while allowing plenty of room
• return to the left as soon as possible without cutting in
• take extra care at night and in poor visibility, when judging speed and distance is harder
• give way to oncoming vehicles before passing parked vehicles or other obstructions on your side
• overtake on the left only when the vehicle ahead is signalling to turn right and there is room
• remain in your lane when traffic is moving slowly in queues. If the queue on your right is moving more slowly, you may pass on the left.

Cyclists may pass slow-moving or stationary traffic on either side. They should proceed cautiously because drivers may not see them, particularly near junctions and when passing lorries or other large vehicles.

Give motorcyclists, cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles at least as much room as you would give a car.

As a guide:

• leave at least 1.5 metres when overtaking cyclists at speeds up to 30 mph, and allow more space at higher speeds
• pass horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles at under 10 mph and leave at least 2 metres
• leave at least 2 metres and keep to a low speed when passing a pedestrian walking in the road, such as where there is no pavement
• take extra care and allow more space when passing motorcyclists, cyclists, horse riders, horse-drawn vehicles or pedestrians in bad weather, including high winds, and at night.

Wait behind and do not overtake a motorcyclist, cyclist, horse rider, horse-drawn vehicle or pedestrian if overtaking is unsafe or the required clearances cannot be achieved.

Remember: Mirrors – Signal – Manoeuvre.

Rule 164

Large vehicles

Overtaking large vehicles is more difficult. You should:

• drop back to improve your view ahead and allow the large-vehicle driver to see you in their mirrors
• remember that following large vehicles too closely, including agricultural vehicles such as tractors with trailers or fixed equipment, obscures your view and may hide another slow-moving vehicle ahead
• ensure that you have enough room to complete the manoeuvre before committing, as passing a large vehicle takes longer
• not overtake if in doubt
• not assume that you can follow a vehicle overtaking a long vehicle, because it may abandon the manoeuvre and pull back in.

Rule 165

You MUST NOT overtake:

• if you would need to cross or straddle double white lines with a solid line nearest you, subject to the exceptions in Rule 129
• if you would need to enter a traffic-separation area bordered by a solid white line
• the vehicle nearest to a pedestrian crossing, especially when it has stopped for pedestrians
• if you would need to enter a lane reserved for buses, trams or cycles during its operating hours
• after a ‘No Overtaking’ sign and before a sign cancels the restriction.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 1; Schedule 9, Part 7; and Schedule 14, Part 1.

Rule 166

DO NOT overtake if you are in doubt or cannot see far enough ahead to know that it is safe, including when approaching:

• a corner or bend
• a hump bridge
• the brow of a hill.

Rule 167

DO NOT overtake where this could bring you into conflict with another road user, including:

• when approaching or at a junction on either side of the road
• where the road narrows
• when approaching a school crossing patrol
• when approaching crossing facilities
• where a vehicle ahead is slowing to stop for a pedestrian crossing from a pedestrian island — see Rule 165
• between the kerb and a bus or tram at a stop
• where traffic is queuing at junctions or roadworks
• where you would force another road user to swerve or slow down
• at a level crossing
• when a road user is signalling right, even if you think the signal should have been cancelled. Wait until it is cancelled
• when following a cyclist approaching a roundabout or junction and you intend to turn left. Stay behind and do not cut across cyclists travelling ahead, including those using cycle lanes or tracks — see Rule H3
• when following a horse rider or horse-drawn vehicle approaching a roundabout or junction and you intend to turn left. Stay behind and do not cut across them
• when a tram is standing at a kerbside tram stop and there is no clearly marked passing lane.

Rule 168

Being overtaken

When another driver is overtaking you:

• maintain a steady course and speed
• slow down if necessary to let the vehicle pass
• never obstruct a driver wishing to pass
• do not speed up or drive unpredictably, as this is dangerous.

If someone overtakes and enters the gap ahead of you, drop back to restore a two-second following gap.

Rule 169

Do not hold up a long queue of traffic, especially when driving a large or slow-moving vehicle.

Check your mirrors frequently and, if necessary, pull in at a safe place to let traffic pass.

category: The Highway Code. 9. Using the road (159 to 203)
description:
Road junctions (Rules 170 to 183)

Rule 170

Take extra care at junctions. You should:

• watch for cyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and powered wheelchair or mobility scooter users, as they may be difficult to see and may not have seen or heard you approaching from behind
• give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross a road into which or from which you are turning. Pedestrians who have started crossing have priority — see Rule H2
• remain behind cyclists, horse riders, horse-drawn vehicles and motorcyclists at junctions, even if they are waiting to turn and are close to the kerb
• watch for long vehicles turning ahead, as they may need the entire width of the road — see Rule 221
• watch for horse riders, who may take a different road position from the one you expect
• not assume that a vehicle approaching from the right and signalling left will turn; wait and make sure
• look all around before emerging
• not cross or join a road until there is a gap large enough to do so safely.

Rule 171

You MUST stop behind the line at a junction with a ‘Stop’ sign and solid white line across the road. Wait for a safe gap in traffic before moving off.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 9, Parts 7 and 8.

Rule 172

The approach to a junction may have a ‘Give Way’ sign or a triangle marked on the road.

You MUST give way to traffic on the main road when emerging from a junction with broken white lines across the road.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 9, Parts 7 and 8.

Rule 173

Dual carriageways

When crossing a dual carriageway or turning right, first assess whether the central reservation is deep enough to protect the full length of your vehicle.

If it is deep enough, treat each half of the carriageway as a separate road. Wait in the central reservation until there is a safe gap in traffic on the second half.

If the central reservation is too shallow for your vehicle, wait until you can cross both carriageways in one movement.

Rule 174

Box junctions

Box junctions have criss-cross yellow lines painted on the road.

You MUST NOT enter a box junction until your exit road or lane is clear.

You may enter and wait in the box when turning right if you are prevented from completing the turn only by:

• oncoming traffic
• other vehicles waiting to turn right.

At a signal-controlled roundabout, you MUST NOT enter the box unless you can cross it completely without stopping.

Law: TSRGD Schedule 9, Parts 7 and 8.

Junctions controlled by traffic lights

Rule 175

You MUST stop behind the white stop line across your side of the road unless the traffic light is green.

If the amber light appears, you may continue only if you have already crossed the stop line or are so close that stopping might cause a collision.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 14, Parts 1 and 4.

Rule 176

You MUST NOT move forward over the white line while the red light is showing.

When the light is green, proceed only if there is enough room to clear the junction safely or you are taking up a position to turn right.

If the traffic lights are not working, treat the junction as unmarked and proceed with great care.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 14, Parts 1 and 4.

Rule 177

Green filter arrows

A green filter arrow applies only to its filter lane. Do not enter that lane unless you intend to travel in the arrow’s direction.

You may proceed in the arrow’s direction when either the green arrow or the full green light is showing.

Give other traffic, especially cyclists, enough time and room to enter the correct lane.

Rule 178

Advanced stop lines

Some signal-controlled junctions have advanced stop lines that allow cyclists to wait ahead of other traffic.

Motorists, including motorcyclists, MUST stop at the first white line they reach when the lights are amber or red.

At other times, avoid blocking access to or encroaching on the marked cyclist area, including when the junction ahead is blocked.

If your vehicle has crossed the first white line when the signal changes to red, stop as soon as possible and MUST stop at the second white line.

When the green signal appears, give cyclists, including those moving or waiting beside you, enough time and space to move off.

Drivers of large vehicles should stop far enough behind the first white line to see the entire area where cyclists may be waiting, allowing for the blind spot in front of the vehicle.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 14, Part 1.

Turning right

Rule 179

Well before turning right, you should:

• use your mirrors to check the position and movement of traffic behind
• signal right
• position your vehicle just left of the centre of the road or in the marked right-turn area
• leave room for other vehicles to pass on the left where possible.

Rule 180

Wait for a safe gap in oncoming traffic. Watch for cyclists, motorcyclists, pedestrians and other road users.

Check your mirrors and blind spot again to ensure that you are not being overtaken, then turn. Do not cut the corner.

Take great care when turning into a main road. Watch for traffic in both directions and wait for a safe gap.

Remember: Mirrors – Signal – Manoeuvre.

Rule 181

When you and an oncoming vehicle are both turning right at crossroads, there are two methods:

• right side to right side — keep the other vehicle on your right and turn behind it. This is generally safer because you have a clear view of approaching traffic when completing the turn
• left side to left side — turn in front of each other. This can obstruct your view of oncoming vehicles, particularly cyclists and motorcyclists, so take extra care.

The road layout, road markings or the other vehicle’s position may determine which method to use.

Turning left

Rule 182

Before turning left:

• use your mirrors
• signal left well before the turn
• do not overtake immediately before turning
• watch for traffic approaching on your left, particularly when driving a large vehicle.

Cyclists, motorcyclists and other road users may be hidden from view.

Rule 183

When turning:

• keep as close to the left as is safe and practicable
• give way to vehicles using a bus lane, cycle lane, cycle track or tramway from either direction, including vehicles passing stationary or slow-moving traffic on either side.

category: The Highway Code. 9. Using the road (159 to 203)
description:
Roundabouts (Rules 184 to 190)

Rule 184

When approaching a roundabout, observe and act on all available information, including traffic signs, traffic lights and lane markings directing you into the correct lane.

You should:

• use Mirrors – Signal – Manoeuvre throughout
• decide as early as possible which exit you need
• give the appropriate signal — see Rule 186
• time your signals so that they do not confuse other road users
• enter the correct lane
• adjust your speed and position to suit traffic conditions
• remain aware of the speed and position of all road users around you.

Rule 185

When reaching a roundabout, you should:

• give priority to traffic approaching from the right unless signs, road markings or traffic lights direct otherwise
• check whether road markings allow you to enter without giving way; if they do, proceed but still look right before joining
• watch for every road user already on the roundabout, remembering that they may signal incorrectly or not signal
• look forward before moving off to ensure that traffic ahead has moved.

Rule 186

Signals and position

When taking the first exit to the left, unless signs or markings indicate otherwise:

• signal left and approach in the left-hand lane
• keep left on the roundabout
• continue signalling left while leaving.

When taking an exit to the right or travelling fully around the roundabout, unless signs or markings indicate otherwise:

• signal right and approach in the right-hand lane
• keep right on the roundabout until you need to change lanes for your exit
• signal left after passing the exit immediately before the one you intend to take.

When taking an intermediate exit, unless signs or markings indicate otherwise:

• select the appropriate lane on approach
• you should not normally need to signal while approaching
• remain in that lane until you need to alter course to exit
• signal left after passing the exit immediately before the one you intend to take.

If there are more than three lanes at the roundabout entrance, use the most appropriate lane on approach and through the roundabout.

Give priority to cyclists on the roundabout. They travel more slowly than motorised traffic. Give them plenty of room and do not attempt to overtake them within their lane. Allow cyclists to move across your path as they travel around the roundabout.

Cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles may remain in the left-hand lane when continuing across or around the roundabout. They should signal right to indicate that they are not leaving.

When entering a roundabout, take extra care not to cut across cyclists, horse riders or horse-drawn vehicles continuing around in the left-hand lane.

Rule 187

In all cases, watch for and give plenty of room to:

• pedestrians crossing approach and exit roads
• traffic crossing in front of you on the roundabout, especially vehicles intending to leave at the next exit
• traffic straddling lanes or positioned incorrectly
• motorcyclists
• long vehicles, including vehicles towing trailers.

Because of their length, long vehicles may need to take a different course or straddle lanes while approaching or travelling around a roundabout. Watch their signals.

Rule 188

Mini-roundabouts

Approach mini-roundabouts in the same way as normal roundabouts.

All vehicles MUST travel around the central markings, except large vehicles that are physically unable to do so.

Remember that there is less space to manoeuvre and less time to signal at a mini-roundabout.

Avoid making U-turns at mini-roundabouts and beware of other road users doing so.

Laws: RTA 1988 section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 9, Parts 7 and 8.

Rule 189

Double mini-roundabouts

Treat each roundabout separately and give way to traffic approaching from the right.

Rule 190

Multiple roundabouts

At some complex junctions, there may be a series of mini-roundabouts at each intersection. Treat each mini-roundabout separately and follow the normal rules.

category: The Highway Code. 9. Using the road (159 to 203)
description:
Pedestrian crossings (Rules 191 to 199)

Rule 191

You MUST NOT:

• park on a crossing
• park within the area covered by zig-zag lines
• overtake the moving vehicle nearest to a crossing
• overtake the vehicle nearest to a crossing when it has stopped to give way to pedestrians.

Laws: RTRA section 25(5) and TSRGD Schedule 14, Parts 1 and 5.

Rule 192

In slow-moving or queuing traffic, keep crossings completely clear. Blocking a crossing makes it difficult and dangerous for pedestrians to cross.

Do not enter a pedestrian crossing unless you can clear it completely. Do not block advanced stop lines for cyclists.

Rule 193

Take extra care when queuing traffic or incorrectly parked vehicles obstruct your view of either side of a crossing. Pedestrians may be crossing between stationary vehicles.

Rule 194

Give pedestrians plenty of time to cross. Do not harass them by revving your engine or moving forward.

Rule 195

Zebra and parallel crossings

When approaching a zebra crossing:

• watch for pedestrians waiting to cross and be ready to slow down or stop
• you should give way to pedestrians waiting to cross
• you MUST give way when a pedestrian has moved onto the crossing
• allow more stopping time on wet or icy roads
• do not wave, flash your headlights or sound your horn to invite pedestrians across, as another vehicle may be approaching
• be patient and do not sound your horn or rev your engine, as this can be intimidating
• watch for pedestrians approaching from the side.

A zebra crossing with a central island consists of two separate crossings. See Rules 19 and 20.

Parallel crossings resemble zebra crossings but include a cycle route alongside the black-and-white stripes.

When approaching a parallel crossing:

• watch for pedestrians or cyclists waiting to cross and slow down or stop
• you should give way to pedestrians or cyclists waiting to cross
• you MUST give way when a pedestrian or cyclist has moved onto the crossing
• allow more stopping time on wet or icy roads
• do not wave, flash your headlights or sound your horn to invite pedestrians or cyclists across, as another vehicle may be approaching
• be patient and do not sound your horn or rev your engine, as this can be intimidating
• watch for pedestrians or cyclists approaching from the side.

A parallel crossing with a central island consists of two separate crossings. See Rules 19 and 20.

Law: TSRGD Schedule 14, Part 5.

Signal-controlled crossings

Rule 196

Pelican crossings

Pelican crossings are signal-controlled crossings where flashing amber follows the red stop light.

You MUST stop when the red light shows.

When the amber light flashes, you MUST give way to pedestrians on the crossing. If the amber light is flashing and no pedestrians are on the crossing, you may proceed cautiously.

Laws: TSRGD regulation 14 and RTRA section 25(5).

Rule 197

A pelican crossing that runs directly across the road is one crossing, even when it has a central island.

You MUST wait for pedestrians crossing from the other side of the island.

Law: TSRGD regulation 14.

Rule 198

Give way to anyone still crossing after the vehicle signal changes to green. This applies at every crossing.

Rule 199

Toucan, puffin and equestrian crossings

These crossings are similar to pelican crossings, but they do not have a flashing amber phase. Their light sequence for traffic is the same as at ordinary traffic lights.

If a signal-controlled crossing is not working, proceed with extreme caution.

Do not enter a crossing unless you can clear it completely, so that you do not obstruct pedestrians, cyclists or horse riders.

category: The Highway Code. 9. Using the road (159 to 203)
description:
Reversing (Rules 200 to 203)

Rule 200

Choose an appropriate place to manoeuvre.

If you need to turn your vehicle around, wait until you find a safe place. Try not to reverse or turn around on a busy road. Instead, find a quiet side road or drive around a block of side streets.

Rule 201

Do not reverse from a side road into a main road.

When using a driveway, reverse into it and drive out if possible.

Rule 202

Look carefully before you begin reversing. You should:

• use all your mirrors
• check the blind spot behind you, which is the part of the road that cannot easily be seen in the mirrors
• check that there are no pedestrians, particularly children, cyclists, other road users or obstructions behind you.

Reverse slowly while:

• checking all around
• looking mainly through the rear window
• remembering that the front of your vehicle will swing out as you turn.

Ask someone to guide you if you cannot see clearly.

Rule 203

You MUST NOT reverse your vehicle farther than necessary.

Law: CUR regulation 106.

category: The Highway Code. 10. Road users requiring extra care (204 to 225)
description:
Overview (Rule 204)

The road users most at risk from road traffic are:

• pedestrians, particularly children, older adults and disabled people
• cyclists
• horse riders
• motorcyclists.

It is particularly important to be aware of:

• children
• older adults
• disabled people
• learner and inexperienced drivers and riders.

In any interaction between road users, those capable of causing the greatest harm have the greatest responsibility to reduce the danger or threat they pose to others.

category: The Highway Code. 10. Road users requiring extra care (204 to 225)
description:
Pedestrians (Rules 205 to 210)

Rule 205

Pedestrians, especially children, may step unexpectedly into the road. Drive with children’s safety in mind and at a speed suitable for the conditions.

Rule 206

Drive carefully and slowly when:

• travelling through crowded shopping streets, Home Zones, Quiet Lanes — see Rule 218 — or residential areas
• passing bus or tram stops, where pedestrians may emerge suddenly into the road
• passing parked vehicles, particularly ice-cream vans, as children may focus on the ice cream rather than traffic and run into the road unexpectedly
• crossing a pavement, cycle lane or cycle track to enter or leave a driveway or private access. Give way to pedestrians on the pavement and cyclists using the cycle lane or track
• reversing into a side road. Look all around your vehicle and give way to pedestrians who may be crossing
• turning at a junction. Give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross the road into which or from which you are turning
• travelling through roadworks or passing roadside rescue and recovery vehicles, as people may be working in or beside the road
• a pavement is closed for street repairs and pedestrians have been directed into the road
• approaching pedestrians on a narrow rural road without a footway or footpath. Slow down, be prepared to stop and give them plenty of room when passing
• approaching zebra or parallel crossings. You MUST give way to pedestrians and cyclists on the crossing — see Rule 195
• approaching pedestrians who have already begun crossing ahead. Pedestrians crossing at a junction or side road have priority, so give way — see Rule H2.

Law: TSRGD Schedule 14, Part 5.

Rule 207

Particularly vulnerable pedestrians

Particularly vulnerable pedestrians include:

• children and older pedestrians, who may be unable to judge your speed and may step into the road
• older pedestrians, who may need more time to cross. Be patient and allow them to cross at their own pace. Do not hurry them by revving the engine or moving forward
• people with disabilities. People with hearing impairments may not know that your vehicle is approaching, while people with walking difficulties need more time
• blind or partially sighted people, who may carry a white cane or use a guide dog and may not see you approaching
• deafblind people, who may carry a white cane with a red band or use a dog wearing a red-and-white harness. They may not see or hear instructions or signals.

At 40 mph (64 km/h), your vehicle will probably kill a pedestrian it hits. At 20 mph (32 km/h), there is only a 1-in-20 chance that the pedestrian will be killed. Therefore, reduce your speed.

Rule 208

Near schools

Drive slowly and be especially aware of young cyclists and pedestrians.

A flashing amber signal may appear below a ‘School’ warning sign to indicate that children may be crossing ahead. Drive very slowly until you have cleared the area.

Rule 209

Drive carefully and slowly when passing a stationary bus displaying a ‘School Bus’ sign, as children may be getting on or off.

Rule 210

You MUST stop when a school crossing patrol displays a ‘Stop for children’ sign. See ‘Signals by authorised persons’ and ‘Traffic signs’.

Law: RTRA section 28.

category: The Highway Code. 10. Road users requiring extra care (204 to 225)
description:
Motorcyclists and cyclists (Rules 211 to 213)

Rule 211

Motorcyclists and cyclists can be difficult to see, especially when they are:

• waiting beside your vehicle
• approaching from behind
• emerging or moving off from junctions
• travelling around roundabouts
• overtaking you
• filtering through traffic.

Always watch for motorcyclists and cyclists before emerging from a junction. They may be approaching faster than you expect.

Do not turn at a junction if doing so would cause a cyclist travelling straight ahead to stop or swerve. Treat the cyclist as you would another motor vehicle.

When turning right across a line of slow-moving or stationary traffic, watch for and give way to cyclists or motorcyclists travelling on the inside of the traffic you are crossing.

Take particular care when moving off, turning, changing direction or changing lanes. Check your mirrors and blind spots carefully.

Rule 212

Give motorcyclists, cyclists, horse riders, horse-drawn vehicles and pedestrians walking in the road, such as where there is no pavement, at least as much room as you would when overtaking a car. See Rules 162 to 167.

Take extra care and allow more space when overtaking these road users:

• in bad weather, including high winds
• at night.

If a rider looks over their shoulder, they may intend to pull out, turn right or change direction. Give them enough time and space to do so.

Rule 213

Cyclists may sometimes ride in the centre of a lane rather than near the side of the road:

• on narrow sections of road
• on quiet roads or streets
• at road junctions
• in slow-moving traffic.

In these situations, it may be safer for groups of cyclists to ride two abreast. Allow them to do so for their safety and so they can see and be seen.

Cyclists are also advised to ride at least a door’s width or 1 metre from parked vehicles for their safety.

Horse riders may ride in the centre of the lane on narrow sections of road. Allow them to do so for their safety and so that they can see and be seen.

Motorcyclists, cyclists, horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles may need to change direction suddenly to avoid uneven road surfaces or obstacles such as:

• drain covers
• oily patches
• wet patches
• icy patches.

Give these road users plenty of room and pay particular attention to any sudden change of direction they may need to make.

category: The Highway Code. 10. Road users requiring extra care (204 to 225)
description:
Other road users (Rules 214 to 218)

Rule 214

Animals

When passing animals:

• drive slowly
• give them plenty of room
• be ready to stop
• do not frighten them by sounding your horn, revving your engine or accelerating rapidly after passing.

Watch for animals being led, driven or ridden on the road and take extra care.

Keep your speed low at bends and on narrow country roads.

If a herd of animals blocks the road, stop and switch off your engine until the animals have left the road.

Watch for animals on unfenced roads.

Rule 215

Horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles

Take particular care around horse riders and horse-drawn vehicles when approaching, overtaking, passing or moving away. Always pass widely and slowly.

When you see a horse on the road:

• reduce your speed to no more than 10 mph
• be patient
• do not sound your horn or rev your engine
• when safe, pass widely and slowly, leaving at least 2 metres of space.

Feral or semi-feral ponies in areas such as the New Forest, Exmoor and Dartmoor require the same consideration as ridden horses when you approach or pass them.

Horse riders are often children, so take extra care. Riders may travel in double file while escorting a young or inexperienced horse or rider.

Watch for signals from horse riders and drivers of horse-drawn vehicles. Follow any request to slow down or stop.

Treat every horse as a potential hazard. Horses can behave unpredictably despite the rider’s or driver’s efforts. Remember that three brains are at work when you pass a horse: the rider’s, the driver’s and the horse’s.

Horses are flight animals and may move extremely quickly if startled.

Rule 216

Older drivers

Older drivers may react more slowly than other drivers. Make allowance for this.

Rule 217

Learners and inexperienced drivers

Learner and inexperienced drivers may be less skilled at anticipating and responding to events.

Be particularly patient with learner drivers and young drivers.

Drivers who have recently passed their test may display a ‘new driver’ plate or sticker. See ‘Safety code for new drivers’.

Rule 218

Home Zones and Quiet Lanes

In Home Zones and Quiet Lanes, people may use the entire road for activities such as children playing or community events.

Drive slowly and carefully. Be prepared to stop and give people additional time to make enough space for you to pass safely.

category: The Highway Code. 10. Road users requiring extra care (204 to 225)
description:
Other vehicles (Rules 219 to 225)

Rule 219

Emergency and incident-support vehicles

Look and listen for:

• ambulances, fire engines, police vehicles, doctors or other emergency vehicles using flashing blue, red or green lights, sirens or flashing headlights
• traffic officer and incident-support vehicles using flashing amber lights.

When one approaches:

• do not panic
• consider the route it is likely to take
• take appropriate action to let it pass while obeying all traffic signs
• if necessary, pull to the side of the road and stop
• try not to stop before the brow of a hill, a bend or a narrow section of road
• do not endanger yourself, other road users or pedestrians
• avoid mounting the kerb
• do not brake harshly when approaching a junction or roundabout, as a following driver may not have the same view as you.

Rule 220

Powered vehicles used by disabled people

These small vehicles have a maximum speed of 8 mph (12 km/h).

On a dual carriageway with a speed limit above 50 mph (80 km/h), they MUST display a flashing amber beacon. On other roads, you may not receive this advance warning. See Rules 36 to 46.

Law: RVLR regulations 17(1) and 26.

Rule 221

Large vehicles

Large vehicles may need additional road space to turn or avoid a hazard that you cannot see.

When following a large vehicle, such as a bus or articulated lorry, remember that its driver may not be able to see you in the mirrors.

Be prepared to stop and wait if the large vehicle needs additional room or time to turn.

Rule 222

Large vehicles can obstruct your view. Pull back and increase your separation distance to improve your ability to see and plan ahead.

Be patient because larger vehicles are subject to lower speed limits than cars and motorcycles.

Many large vehicles may have speed-limiting devices that restrict them to 56 mph (90 km/h), even on a motorway.

Rule 223

Buses, coaches and trams

Give priority to buses, coaches and trams when you can do so safely, particularly when they signal to pull away from stops.

Watch for people leaving a bus or tram and crossing the road.

Rule 224

Electric vehicles

Take care around electric vehicles such as milk floats and trams.

Trams travel quickly but quietly and cannot steer to avoid you.

Rule 225

Vehicles with flashing amber beacons

A flashing amber beacon warns of:

• a slow-moving or stationary vehicle, such as a traffic officer vehicle, salt spreader, snowplough or recovery vehicle
• an abnormal load.

Approach these vehicles cautiously.

On unrestricted dual carriageways, motor vehicles first used on or after 1 January 1947 that have a maximum speed of 25 mph (40 km/h) or less, such as tractors, MUST use a flashing amber beacon. See also Rule 220.

Law: RVLR regulation 17.

category: The Highway Code. 11. Driving in adverse weather conditions (226 to 237)
description:
Overview (Rule 226)

You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced. Visibility is generally considered seriously reduced when you cannot see farther than 100 metres (328 feet).

You may also use front or rear fog lights, but you MUST switch them off when visibility improves. See Rule 236.

Law: RVLR regulations 25 and 27.

category: The Highway Code. 11. Driving in adverse weather conditions (226 to 237)
description:
Wet weather (Rule 227)

In wet weather, stopping distances are at least double those required on dry roads. See ‘Typical stopping distances’. This is because tyres have less grip on a wet road.

In wet weather:

• keep well back from the vehicle ahead to improve your ability to see and plan ahead
• if the steering becomes unresponsive, water is probably preventing the tyres from gripping the road. Ease off the accelerator and slow down gradually
• remember that rain and spray from vehicles may make it difficult to see and be seen
• be aware that spilt diesel can make the road surface extremely slippery — see ‘Vehicle maintenance, safety and security’
• take extra care around pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists and horse riders.

category: The Highway Code. 11. Driving in adverse weather conditions (226 to 237)
description:
Icy and snowy weather (Rules 228 to 231)

Rule 228

During winter, check the local weather forecast for warnings of icy or snowy conditions.

DO NOT drive in these conditions unless your journey is essential. If you must travel, take great care and allow additional time.

Carry an emergency kit containing:

• de-icer and an ice scraper
• a torch
• warm clothing and boots
• a first-aid kit
• jump leads
• a shovel
• a warm drink
• emergency food.

These supplies may be needed if you become stuck or your vehicle breaks down.

Rule 229

Before setting off:

• you MUST be able to see, so remove all snow and ice from every window and ensure that the windscreen is completely clear
• you MUST ensure that the lights are clean
• you MUST ensure that the number plates are clearly visible and legible
• ensure that the mirrors are clear and the windows are thoroughly demisted
• remove all snow that might fall into the path of another road user
• check that your planned route is clear of delays and that no additional snowfall or severe weather is forecast.

Laws: CUR regulation 30; RVLR regulation 23; VERA section 43; and RV(DRM)R regulation 11.

Rule 230

When driving in icy or snowy conditions:

• drive carefully even when the roads have been treated
• keep well back from the road user ahead, as stopping distances may be ten times greater than on dry roads
• take care when overtaking vehicles spreading salt or other de-icer, especially when riding a motorcycle or cycle
• watch for snowploughs, which may throw snow to either side
• do not overtake a snowplough unless the lane you intend to use has been cleared
• be prepared for road conditions to change over relatively short distances
• listen to travel bulletins and observe variable-message signs for information about the weather, road and traffic conditions ahead.

Rule 231

Drive extremely carefully on icy roads and avoid sudden actions, which could cause loss of control.

You should:

• drive slowly in as high a gear as possible
• accelerate and brake very gently
• drive particularly slowly on bends, where loss of control is more likely
• brake progressively while travelling straight before reaching a bend
• after slowing, steer smoothly around the bend and avoid sudden actions
• test your grip on snow or ice by choosing a safe place and braking gently.

Unresponsive steering may indicate ice and loss of tyre grip. Tyres make almost no noise while travelling on ice.

category: The Highway Code. 11. Driving in adverse weather conditions (226 to 237)
description:
Windy weather (Rules 232 to 233)

Rule 232

High-sided vehicles are most affected by windy weather, but strong gusts can also blow a car, cyclist, motorcyclist or horse rider off course. This can happen on open stretches of road exposed to strong crosswinds, or when passing bridges or gaps in hedges.

Rule 233

In very windy weather, your vehicle may be affected by turbulence created by large vehicles. Motorcyclists are particularly affected, so keep well back from them when they are overtaking a high-sided vehicle.

category: The Highway Code. 11. Driving in adverse weather conditions (226 to 237)
description:
Fog (Rules 234 to 236)

Rule 234

Before entering fog, check your mirrors and then slow down.

If ‘Fog’ is shown on a sign but the road is clear, be prepared for a bank of fog or drifting patchy fog ahead. Even if it seems to be clearing, you can suddenly find yourself in thick fog.

Rule 235

When driving in fog, you should:

• use your lights as required (see Rule 226)
• keep a safe distance behind the vehicle in front; rear lights can give a false sense of security
• be able to pull up well within the distance you can see clearly. This is particularly important on motorways and dual carriageways, as vehicles are travelling faster
• use your windscreen wipers and demisters
• beware of other drivers not using headlights
• not accelerate to get away from a vehicle which is too close behind you
• check your mirrors before you slow down. Then use your brakes so that your brake lights warn drivers behind you that you are slowing down
• stop in the correct position at a junction with limited visibility and listen for traffic. When you are sure it is safe to emerge, do so positively and do not hesitate in a position that puts you directly in the path of approaching vehicles.

Rule 236

You MUST NOT use front or rear fog lights unless visibility is seriously reduced (see Rule 226), as they dazzle other road users and can obscure your brake lights. You MUST switch them off when visibility improves.

Law: RVLR Regulations 25 and 27.

category: The Highway Code. 11. Driving in adverse weather conditions (226 to 237)
description:
Hot weather (Rule 237)

Rule 237

Keep your vehicle well ventilated to avoid drowsiness.

Be aware that the road surface may become soft or, if it rains after a dry spell, it may become slippery. These conditions could affect your steering and braking.

If you are dazzled by bright sunlight, slow down and, if necessary, stop.

category: The Highway Code. 12. Waiting and parking (238 to 252)
description:
General (Rule 238)

Rule 238

You MUST NOT wait or park on yellow lines during the times of operation shown on nearby time plates, or on zone entry signs if you are in a Controlled Parking Zone. See ‘Traffic signs’ and ‘Road markings’.

Double yellow lines indicate that waiting is prohibited at all times, even if there are no upright signs.

You MUST NOT wait, park or stop to set down or pick up passengers on school entrance markings when upright signs indicate that stopping is prohibited.

Law: RTRA Sections 5 and 8.

category: The Highway Code. 12. Waiting and parking (238 to 252)
description:
Parking (Rules 239 to 247)

Rule 239

Use off-street parking areas, or bays marked out with white lines on the road as parking places, wherever possible.

If you have to stop on the roadside:

• do not park facing against the traffic flow
• stop as close as you can to the side
• do not stop too close to a vehicle displaying a Blue Badge; remember, the occupant may need more room to get in or out
• you MUST switch off the engine, headlights and fog lights
• you MUST apply the handbrake before leaving the vehicle
• you MUST ensure you do not hit anyone when you open your door. Check for cyclists or other traffic by looking all around and using your mirrors
• where you are able to do so, you should open the door using your hand on the opposite side to the door you are opening; for example, use your left hand to open a door on your right-hand side. This will make you turn your head to look over your shoulder. You are then more likely to avoid causing injury to cyclists or motorcyclists passing you on the road, or to people on the pavement
• it is safer for your passengers, especially children, to get out of the vehicle on the side next to the kerb
• put all valuables out of sight and make sure your vehicle is secure
• lock your vehicle.

Before using a hand-held device to help you park, you MUST make sure it is safe to do so. You should then move the vehicle into the parking space in the safest way and by the shortest route possible.

When you use a hand-held device to help you park, you MUST remain in control of the vehicle at all times. Do not use the hand-held device for anything else while using it to help you park, and do not put anyone in danger. Use the device according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

When using an electric vehicle charge point, you should park close to the charge point and avoid creating a trip hazard for pedestrians with trailing cables. Display a warning sign if you can. After using the charge point, you should return charging cables and connectors neatly to minimise danger to pedestrians and avoid creating an obstacle for other road users.

Laws: CUR Regulations 98, 105, 107 and 110; RVLR Regulation 27; and RTA 1988 Section 42.

Rule 240

You MUST NOT stop or park on:

• the carriageway, an emergency area or a hard shoulder of a motorway, except in an emergency (see Rules 270 and 271)
• a pedestrian crossing, including the area marked by zig-zag lines (see Rule 191)
• a clearway (see ‘Traffic signs’)
• taxi bays, as indicated by upright signs and markings
• an urban clearway within its hours of operation, except to pick up or set down passengers (see ‘Traffic signs’)
• a road marked with double white lines, even when a broken white line is on your side of the road, except to pick up or set down passengers or to load or unload goods
• a tram or cycle lane during its period of operation
• a cycle track
• red lines on specially designated ‘red routes’, unless signs indicate otherwise.

Any vehicle may enter a bus lane to stop, load or unload where this is not prohibited (see Rule 141).

Laws: MT(E&W)R Regulations 7 and 9 as amended by MT(E&W)(A)(E)R; MT(S)R Regulations 6 and 8; RTRA Sections 5, 6 and 8; and TSRGD Schedule 7, Parts 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7, Schedule 9, Part 6, and Schedule 14, Parts 1 and 5.

Rule 241

You MUST NOT park in spaces reserved for specific users, such as Blue Badge holders, residents or motorcycles, unless you are entitled to do so.

Laws: CSDPA Section 21 and RTRA Sections 5 and 8.

Rule 242

You MUST NOT leave your vehicle or trailer in a dangerous position or where it causes any unnecessary obstruction of the road.

Laws: RTA 1988 Section 22 and CUR Regulation 103.

Rule 243

Except when forced to do so by stationary traffic, DO NOT stop or park:

• near a school entrance
• anywhere you would prevent access for Emergency Services
• at or near a bus or tram stop or taxi rank
• on the approach to a level crossing or tramway crossing
• opposite or within 10 metres (32 feet) of a junction, except in an authorised parking space
• near the brow of a hill or a hump bridge
• opposite a traffic island or, if this would cause an obstruction, another parked vehicle
• where you would force other traffic to enter a tram lane
• where the kerb has been lowered to help wheelchair users and powered mobility vehicles
• in front of an entrance to a property
• on a bend
• where you would obstruct cyclists’ use of cycle facilities.

In Scotland, you MUST NOT double park or park anywhere the kerb has been lowered to help pedestrians or cyclists. Exceptions are allowed in limited circumstances.

Law: T(Scot)A Part 6.

Rule 244

You MUST NOT park partially or wholly on the pavement in London or Scotland. Exceptions are allowed in limited circumstances. Elsewhere, you should not park partially or wholly on the pavement unless signs permit it.

Parking on the pavement can obstruct and seriously inconvenience pedestrians, people in wheelchairs or with visual impairments, and people with prams or pushchairs.

Laws: GL(GP)A Section 15 and T(Scot)A Part 6.

Rule 245

Controlled Parking Zones

Zone entry signs indicate the times when waiting restrictions within the zone are in force. Parking may be allowed in some places at other times. Otherwise, parking will be within separately signed and marked bays.

Rule 246

Goods vehicles

Vehicles with a maximum laden weight of over 7.5 tonnes, including any trailer, MUST NOT be parked on a verge, pavement or any land situated between carriageways without police permission.

The only exception is when parking is essential for loading or unloading, in which case the vehicle MUST NOT be left unattended.

Law: RTA 1988 Section 19.

Rule 247

Loading and unloading

Do not load or unload where there are yellow markings on the kerb and upright signs advise that restrictions are in place (see ‘Road markings’). Loading or unloading may be permitted where parking is otherwise restricted.

On red routes, specially marked and signed bays indicate where and when loading and unloading is permitted.

Law: RTRA Sections 5 and 8.

category: The Highway Code. 12. Waiting and parking (238 to 252)
description:
Parking at night (Rules 248 to 252)

Rule 248

You MUST NOT park on a road at night facing against the direction of the traffic flow unless you are in a recognised parking space.

Laws: CUR Regulation 101 and RVLR Regulation 24.

Rule 249

All vehicles MUST display parking lights when parked on a road or in a lay-by on a road with a speed limit greater than 30 mph (48 km/h).

Law: RVLR Regulation 24.

Rule 250

Cars, goods vehicles not exceeding 2,500 kg laden weight, invalid carriages, motorcycles and pedal cycles may be parked without lights on a road or in a lay-by with a speed limit of 30 mph (48 km/h) or less if they are:

• at least 10 metres (32 feet) away from any junction, close to the kerb and facing in the direction of the traffic flow
• in a recognised parking place or lay-by.

Other vehicles and trailers, and all vehicles with projecting loads, MUST NOT be left on a road at night without lights.

Laws: RVLR Regulation 24 and CUR Regulation 82(7).

Rule 251

Parking in fog

It is especially dangerous to park on the road in fog. If it is unavoidable, leave your parking lights or sidelights on.

Rule 252

Parking on hills

If you park on a hill, you should:

• park close to the kerb and apply the handbrake firmly
• select a forward gear and turn your steering wheel away from the kerb when facing uphill
• select reverse gear and turn your steering wheel towards the kerb when facing downhill
• use ‘park’ if your car has an automatic gearbox.

category: The Highway Code. 12. Waiting and parking (238 to 252)
description:
Decriminalised Parking Enforcement (DPE)

DPE is becoming increasingly common as more authorities take on this role. Under DPE, the local traffic authority assumes responsibility for enforcing many parking contraventions in place of the police.

Further details on DPE may be found at:

• Traffic Penalty Tribunal (outside London): http://www.trafficpenaltytribunal.gov.uk/
• London Tribunals (inside London): http://www.londontribunals.gov.uk/

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
General (Rules 253 to 254)

Rule 253

Prohibited vehicles

Motorways MUST NOT be used by:

• pedestrians
• holders of provisional motorcycle licences
• riders of motorcycles under 50 cc (4 kW)
• cyclists
• horse riders
• certain slow-moving vehicles
• vehicles carrying oversized loads, except with special permission
• agricultural vehicles
• powered wheelchairs and powered mobility scooters (see Rules 36 to 46 inclusive).

Provisional car licence holders MUST NOT drive on a motorway unless they:

• are accompanied by a DVSA Approved Driving Instructor (ADI)
• are driving a car displaying red L plates, or D plates in Wales
• are driving a car fitted with dual controls.

Laws: HA 1980 Sections 16 and 17 and Schedule 4; MT(E&W)R Regulations 3(d), 4 and 11 as amended by MT(E&W)(A)R 2004 and MT(E&W)(A)R 2018; R(S)A Sections 7 and 8 and Schedule 3; RTRA Section 17; and MT(S)R Regulation 10 as amended by MT(S)(A)R 2018.

Rule 254

Traffic on motorways usually travels faster than on other roads, so you have less time to react. It is especially important to use your mirrors earlier and look much further ahead than you would on other roads.

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
Motorway signals (Rules 255 to 258)

Rule 255

Signs and signals (see ‘Light signals controlling traffic’) are used to warn you of hazards ahead. For example, there may be an incident, fog, a spillage or road workers on the carriageway that you may not immediately be able to see.

Rule 256

A single sign or signal can display advice, restrictions and warnings for all lanes.

Lane-specific signs and signals can display advice, restrictions and warnings that apply to individual lanes.

Rule 257

Amber flashing lights

These signals warn of a hazard ahead. You should:

• reduce your speed
• be prepared for the hazard
• only increase your speed when you pass a signal that is not flashing, or a sign displaying a national speed limit or the word ‘END’, and you are sure it is safe to do so.

Rule 258

Red flashing light signals and a red ‘X’ on a sign identify a closed lane in which people, stopped vehicles or other hazards are present.

You:

• MUST follow the instructions on signs in advance of a closed lane to move safely to an open lane
• MUST NOT drive in a closed lane.

A sign will inform you when the lane is no longer closed by displaying a speed limit or the word ‘END’.

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
Joining the motorway (Rule 259)

Rule 259

When you join a motorway, you will normally approach it from a road on the left, called a slip road, or from an adjoining motorway.

You should:

• give priority to traffic already on the motorway
• check the traffic on the motorway and match your speed to fit safely into the traffic flow in the left-hand lane
• not cross solid white lines separating lanes or use the hard shoulder
• stay on the slip road if it continues as an extra lane on the motorway
• remain in the left-hand lane long enough to adjust to the speed of traffic before considering overtaking.

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
On the motorway (Rules 260 to 263)

Rule 260

When you can see well ahead and the road conditions are good, you should:

• drive at a steady cruising speed that you and your vehicle can handle safely and that is within the speed limit (see Rule 124 and the Speed limits table)
• keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front and increase the gap on wet or icy roads, or in fog (see Rules 126 and 235).

Rule 261

You MUST NOT exceed:

• a speed limit displayed within a red circle on a sign
• the maximum speed limit for the road and for your vehicle (see Rule 124).

Speed limits are enforced by the police (see Rule 124).

Law: RTRA Sections 17, 86 and 89 and Schedule 6.

Rule 262

The monotony of driving on motorways and other high-speed roads can make you feel sleepy. To minimise the risk, follow the advice in Rule 91 about ensuring that you are fit to drive and taking breaks.

Service areas are located along motorways to allow you to take breaks and obtain refreshments. Refreshment and rest facilities on the local road network may also be accessible from motorway exits.

Rule 263

Unless directed to do so by a police officer or traffic officer, you MUST NOT:

• reverse along any part of a motorway, including slip roads, hard shoulders and emergency areas
• cross the central reservation
• drive against the traffic flow.

If you have missed your exit or taken the wrong route, carry on to the next exit.

Laws: RTA 1988 Section 35 as amended by TMA Section 6; MT(E&W)R Regulations 6, 8 and 10; and MT(S)R Regulations 4, 5, 7 and 9.

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
Lane discipline (Rules 264 to 266)

Rule 264

Keep in the left lane unless overtaking.

If you are overtaking, you should return to the left lane when it is safe to do so (see also Rules 267 and 268).

Be aware of emergency services, traffic officers, recovery workers and other people or vehicles stopped on the hard shoulder or in an emergency area. If you are driving in the left lane and it is safe to do so, you should move into the adjacent lane to create more space between your vehicle and the people and stopped vehicles.

Rule 265

The right-hand lane of a motorway with three or more lanes MUST NOT be used, except in prescribed circumstances, if you are driving:

• any vehicle drawing a trailer
• a goods vehicle with a maximum laden weight exceeding 3.5 tonnes but not exceeding 7.5 tonnes that is required to be fitted with a speed limiter
• a goods vehicle with a maximum laden weight exceeding 7.5 tonnes
• a passenger vehicle with a maximum laden weight exceeding 7.5 tonnes, constructed or adapted to carry more than eight seated passengers in addition to the driver
• a passenger vehicle with a maximum laden weight not exceeding 7.5 tonnes, constructed or adapted to carry more than eight seated passengers in addition to the driver, that is required to be fitted with a speed limiter.

Laws: MT(E&W)R Regulation 12, MT(E&W)(A)R, MT(S)R Regulation 11 and MT(S)(A)R.

Rule 266

Approaching a junction

Look well ahead for signals, signs and road markings. Direction signs may be placed over the road. If necessary, you should change lanes well ahead of a junction.

At some junctions, a lane may lead directly off the road. Only enter that lane if you wish to travel in the direction indicated by the signs or road markings.

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
Overtaking (Rules 267 to 268)

Rule 267

Do not overtake unless you are sure it is safe and legal to do so. Overtake only on the right.

You should:

• check your mirrors
• take time to judge speeds correctly
• make sure the lane you will be joining is sufficiently clear ahead and behind
• take a quick sideways glance into the blind spot area to verify the position of a vehicle that may have disappeared from your view in the mirror
• remember that traffic may be coming up behind you very quickly. Check all your mirrors carefully and look out for motorcyclists. When it is safe to do so, signal in plenty of time and then move out
• ensure that you do not cut in on the vehicle you have overtaken
• be especially careful at night and in poor visibility, when it is harder to judge speed and distance.

Rule 268

Do not overtake on the left or move to a lane on your left to overtake.

In congested conditions, where adjacent lanes of traffic are moving at similar speeds, traffic in left-hand lanes may sometimes move faster than traffic to the right. In these conditions, you may keep up with the traffic in your lane even if this means passing traffic in the lane to your right.

Do not weave in and out of lanes to overtake.

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
Hard shoulder (Rule 269)

Hard shoulder where present

You MUST NOT use a hard shoulder except:

• in an emergency
• when directed to do so by the police
• when directed to do so by traffic officers
• when directed to do so by a traffic sign.

Hard shoulder where used as an extra lane

The hard shoulder is used as an extra lane on some motorways during periods of congestion.

A red ‘X’ or blank sign above the hard shoulder means that you MUST NOT use the hard shoulder except in an emergency.

You can only use the hard shoulder as an extra lane when a speed limit is shown above it.

Where the hard shoulder is being used as an extra lane, emergency areas are provided for use in an emergency (see Rule 270).

Laws: MT(E&W)R Regulations 5 and 9; MT(S)R Regulations 4 and 8; and RTA 1988 Sections 35 and 36 as amended by TMA Section 6.

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
Stopping (Rules 270 to 272)

Rule 270

Emergency areas are located along motorways with no hard shoulder or where the hard shoulder can be used as an extra lane (see Rule 269). They MUST only be used in an emergency.

Emergency areas are marked by blue signs with an orange SOS telephone symbol and may have orange surfacing.

Follow the requirements and advice in:

• Rule 277 if your vehicle develops a problem on the motorway
• Rule 278 when rejoining the carriageway from an emergency area.

Laws: MT(E&W)R Regulation 9 as amended by MT(E&W)(A)(E)R, and MT(S)R Regulation 8.

Rule 271

You MUST NOT stop on any carriageway, emergency area, hard shoulder, slip road, central reservation or verge except:

• in an emergency
• when told to do so by the police
• when told to do so by traffic officers
• when instructed by an emergency sign
• when instructed by red flashing light signals.

Do not stop on any part of a motorway to make or receive mobile telephone calls, except in an emergency.

Laws: MT(E&W)R Regulations 7, 9, 10 and 16 as amended by MT(E&W)(A)(E)R; MT(S)R Regulations 6(1), 8, 9 and 14; PRA Section 41 and Schedule 5(8); RTA 1988 Sections 35, 36 and 163 as amended by TMA Section 6; and CUR Regulation 110 as amended by CUR(A)(No. 4)R.

Rule 272

You MUST NOT pick up or set down anyone, or walk on a motorway, except in an emergency.

Laws: RTRA Section 17 and MT(E&W)R Regulation 15.

category: The Highway Code. 13. Motorways (253 to 274)
description:
Leaving the motorway (Rules 273 to 274)

Rule 273

Unless signs indicate that a lane leads directly off the motorway, you will normally leave the motorway by a slip road on your left.

You should:

• watch for signs that let you know you are getting near your exit
• move into the left-hand lane well before reaching your exit
• signal left in good time and reduce your speed on the slip road as necessary.

Rule 274

When leaving the motorway or using a link road between motorways, your speed may be higher than you realise. For example, 50 mph may feel like 30 mph.

Check your speedometer and adjust your speed accordingly. Some slip roads and link roads have sharp bends, so you will need to slow down.

category: The Highway Code. 14. Breakdowns and incidents (275 to 287)
description:
Place of relative safety (Rule 275)

Rule 275

If you need to stop your vehicle because of a breakdown or incident, try to stop in a place of relative safety.

A place of relative safety is somewhere that you, your passengers and your vehicle are less likely to be at risk from moving traffic.

The safest place to stop is a location designed for parking. On motorways and other high-speed roads, the safest place to stop is a service area.

Other places of relative safety include:

• lay-bys
• emergency areas (see Rule 270)
• hard shoulders (see Rule 269).

Be aware that hard shoulders provide less protection than other places of relative safety because they are so close to high-speed traffic.

Where possible, you and your passengers should keep well away from your vehicle and moving traffic. Otherwise, moving traffic could collide with your vehicle and force it into you and your passengers.

category: The Highway Code. 14. Breakdowns and incidents (275 to 287)
description:
Breakdowns (Rule 276)

Rule 276

If your vehicle breaks down, think first of all other road users. Get your vehicle off the road if possible. If it causes an obstruction, warn other traffic with your hazard warning lights. In daylight, wear light-coloured or fluorescent clothing; at night or in poor visibility, wear reflective clothing. Place a warning triangle at least 45 metres (147 feet) behind the broken-down vehicle on the same side of the road, or use other permitted warning devices if available. Take great care when placing or retrieving warning devices, and never use them on motorways. If possible, keep your sidelights on when it is dark or visibility is poor. Do not stand or allow anyone else to stand between your vehicle and oncoming traffic. At night or in poor visibility, do not stand where you would prevent other road users from seeing your lights.

category: The Highway Code. 14. Breakdowns and incidents (275 to 287)
description:
Additional rules for motorways (Rules 277 to 279)

Rule 277

If your vehicle develops a problem, leave the carriageway at the next exit or pull into a service area if possible (see Rule 275 for places of relative safety). If you cannot, follow this guidance.

Go left

• move into the left lane
• pull into an emergency area or onto a hard shoulder if you can
• stop as far to the left as possible, leaving space to exit your vehicle and with your wheels turned to the left
• if you can, stop just beyond an emergency telephone
• switch on your hazard warning lights
• if it is dark or visibility is poor, use sidelights.

Get safe

Exit your vehicle by the side furthest from traffic if it is safe and possible to do so, and ensure that passengers do the same.

If you cannot both get your vehicle to the left lane or a place of relative safety (see Rule 275) and exit safely to get well away from your vehicle and moving traffic, you should:

• stay in your vehicle
• keep your seat belts and hazard warning lights on
• call 999 immediately and ask for the police. Alternatively, press your vehicle’s SOS button, if it has one, and ask for the police.

If you can safely leave the vehicle:

• put on high-visibility clothing if you have it and it is within easy reach
• get behind a safety barrier where one is present, but be aware of unseen hazards such as sudden drops, uneven ground or debris
• DO NOT stand where your vehicle could be forced into you if moving traffic collides with it
• DO NOT return to your vehicle, even if it is raining, cold or dark
• remain alert and aware of vehicles or debris coming towards you
• keep passengers away from the carriageway and keep children under control
• DO NOT attempt repairs on your vehicle
• DO NOT place a warning triangle on the carriageway
• animals MUST be kept in the vehicle or, in an emergency, under control on the verge.

Get help

• use the free emergency telephone to obtain advice and assistance
• contact a breakdown recovery service
• always face the traffic while speaking so that you remain aware of vehicles or debris coming towards you
• tell the service if you are a vulnerable motorist, such as someone who is disabled, older or travelling alone
• wait well away from your vehicle and moving traffic, behind the safety barrier where one is present
• if you cannot exit your vehicle or have not stopped near a free emergency telephone, call 999 immediately and ask for the police. Alternatively, press your vehicle’s SOS button, if it has one, and ask for the police.

Communicating your location to the emergency services

• eCall: press the SOS button if your vehicle has one
• app: use a mobile telephone mapping application
• marker post or driver location sign: quote the numbers and letters shown on marker posts or driver location signs located along the edge of the road.

Laws: MT(E&W)R Regulation 14 and MT(S)R Regulation 12.

Rule 278

To rejoin the carriageway after a breakdown from a hard shoulder, build up speed, indicate and watch for a safe gap in the traffic. Be aware that vehicles, obstructions or debris may be present on the hard shoulder.

To rejoin from an emergency area, you MUST use the emergency telephone provided and follow the operator’s advice. A lane may need to be closed so that you can rejoin the carriageway safely.

Law: RTA 1988 Section 36.

Rule 279

Disabled drivers

If you have a disability that prevents you from following the advice in Rules 277 and 278, you should:
