• switch on your hazard warning lights
• stay in your vehicle and keep your seat belt on
• call 999 immediately and ask for the police. Alternatively, press your vehicle’s SOS button, if it has one, and ask for the police.

If you are deaf, hard of hearing or speech impaired, it is recommended that you register for the 999 text service at emergencySMS.net before making a journey.

category: The Highway Code. 14. Breakdowns and incidents (275 to 287)
description:
Obstructions (Rule 280)

Rule 280

If anything falls from a vehicle onto a motorway or another high-speed road, DO NOT remove the obstruction yourself. Stop in a place of relative safety (see Rule 275) and call the emergency services on 999.

On other roads, you should only remove an obstruction if it is safe to do so.

category: The Highway Code. 14. Breakdowns and incidents (275 to 287)
description:
Incidents (Rules 281 to 283)

Rule 281

Warning signs or flashing lights

If you see emergency or incident support vehicles displaying flashing lights in the distance, be aware that there may be an incident ahead (see Rule 219). You should slow down and be prepared to move safely into another lane or stop.

The emergency services, traffic officers and recovery workers may need to work in the carriageway; for example, to deal with debris or collisions or to conduct rolling roadblocks.

You MUST follow any directions given by police or traffic officers about whether you can safely pass the incident or obstruction.

Laws: RTA 1988 Sections 35 and 163 as amended by TMA Section 6.

Rule 282

When passing the scene of an incident, remain alert for hazards such as debris or slow-moving vehicles. Do not slow down unnecessarily; for example, when an incident is on the other side of a dual carriageway.

Focus on the road ahead when passing an incident. A lack of attention may cause another incident, a collision or congestion (see also Rule 283).

Rule 283

If you are involved in an incident or collision, or stop to give assistance:

• if possible, stop in a place of relative safety (see Rule 275)
• use your hazard warning lights to warn other traffic
• put on high-visibility clothing if you have it
• ask drivers to switch off their engines
• ask drivers and passengers to stop smoking
• contact the emergency services on 999 and provide full details of the incident location and any casualties. Use an emergency telephone, a mobile telephone or your vehicle’s SOS button, if it has one. See Rule 277 for how to identify your location on a motorway or other high-speed road
• move uninjured people away from the vehicles to a place of relative safety (see Rule 275)
• DO NOT move injured people from their vehicles unless they are in immediate danger
• DO NOT remove a motorcyclist’s helmet unless it is essential and you are trained to do so
• be prepared to give first aid (see ‘First aid on the road’ and ‘Useful websites’)
• stay at the scene until the emergency services arrive
• be prepared to exchange details (see Rule 286).

If you are involved in any other medical emergency, contact the emergency services in the same way.

category: The Highway Code. 14. Breakdowns and incidents (275 to 287)
description:
Incidents involving dangerous goods (Rules 284 to 285)

Rule 284

Vehicles carrying dangerous goods in packages will be marked with plain orange reflective plates.

Road tankers and vehicles carrying tank containers of dangerous goods will have hazard warning plates (see ‘Vehicle markings’).

Rule 285

If an incident involves a vehicle containing dangerous goods, follow the advice in Rule 283 and, in particular:

• switch off engines and DO NOT SMOKE
• keep well away from the vehicle. Do not be tempted to try to rescue casualties, as you could become a casualty yourself
• call the emergency services and give as much information as possible about the labels and markings on the vehicle
• DO NOT use a mobile phone close to a vehicle carrying flammable loads.

category: The Highway Code. 14. Breakdowns and incidents (275 to 287)
description:
Documentation (Rules 286 to 287)

Rule 286

If you are involved in a collision that causes damage or injury to another person, vehicle, animal or property, you MUST:

• stop. If possible, stop in a place of relative safety (see Rule 275)
• give your own name and address, the vehicle owner’s name and address, and the vehicle’s registration number to anyone who has reasonable grounds for requiring them
• if you do not give your name and address at the time of the collision, report the collision to the police as soon as reasonably practicable and, in any case, within 24 hours.

Law: RTA 1988 Section 170.

Rule 287

If another person is injured and you do not produce your insurance certificate at the time of the collision to a police officer or anyone who has reasonable grounds to request it, you MUST:

• report the collision to the police as soon as possible and, in any case, within 24 hours
• produce your insurance certificate for the police within seven days.

Law: RTA 1988 Section 170.

category: The Highway Code. 15. Road works, level crossings and tramways (288 to 307)
description:
Road works (Rule 288)

Rule 288

When the ‘Road Works Ahead’ sign is displayed, take extra care and look for additional signs providing more specific instructions. Observe all signs, as they are there for your safety and the safety of road workers.

You MUST NOT exceed any temporary maximum speed limit.

Keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front (see Rule 126).

Use your mirrors and get into the correct lane for your vehicle in good time and as signs direct.

Do not switch lanes to overtake queuing traffic.

Take extra care near cyclists and motorcyclists, as they are vulnerable to skidding on grit, mud or other debris at road works.

Where lanes are restricted because of road works, merge in turn (see Rule 134).

Do not drive through an area marked off by traffic cones.

Watch for vehicles entering or leaving the works area. Where vehicles are travelling on the road and displaying amber warning lights, leave extra space and expect them to slow down or turn into a works area.

Concentrate on the road ahead, not on the road works.

Bear in mind that the road ahead may be obstructed by the works or by slow-moving or stationary traffic.

Law: RTRA Section 16.

category: The Highway Code. 15. Road works, level crossings and tramways (288 to 307)
subcategory: Additional rules for high-speed roads (rules 289 to 290)
englishSubcategory: Additional rules for high-speed roads (rules 289 to 290)
description:
Additional rules for high-speed roads (Rules 289 to 290)

Rule 289

Take special care on motorways and other high-speed dual carriageways.

Lanes may be closed to traffic and a lower speed limit may apply.

Works vehicles may be used to close lanes or carriageways for repairs. Where large ‘Keep Left’ or ‘Keep Right’ signs are displayed on the back, you MUST move over and pass the works vehicle on the side indicated. Do not return to the closed lane until you can see that it is safe to do so.

Where a vehicle displays the sign ‘CONVOY VEHICLE NO OVERTAKING’, you MUST NOT pass the vehicle.

A flashing light arrow or red ‘X’ may also be used to make the works vehicle more visible from a distance and provide drivers with an earlier warning.

Laws: RTA 1988 Section 36, TSRGD Regulation 3 and Schedule 13.

Rule 290

Road works may contain features that require extra care.

Narrow lanes

Lanes may be narrower than normal and will be marked by studs or temporary road markings. Keep a safe distance from the vehicle in front (see Rule 126) and make sure that you can clearly see the edges of the lane ahead.

Contraflow systems

In a contraflow system, you may travel in a narrower lane than normal without a permanent barrier between you and oncoming traffic.

At the start and finish of a contraflow, slow down and increase the distance from the vehicle in front because changes in the road’s camber may affect vehicle stability.

Breakdown advice

If your vehicle breaks down in road works, follow Rules 275, 277 and 278, but be aware that areas marked off by cones contain significant hazards.

Where available, move your vehicle into a signed road works refuge location. Signs indicate where dedicated recovery services are provided.

category: The Highway Code. 15. Road works, level crossings and tramways (288 to 307)
description:
Level crossings (Rules 291 to 299)

Rule 291

A level crossing is where a road crosses a railway or tramway line. Approach and cross it with care.

Never drive onto a crossing until the road is clear on the other side, and do not get too close to the vehicle in front. Never stop or park on or near a crossing.

Rule 292

Overhead electric lines

It is dangerous to touch overhead electric lines. You MUST obey safe-height warning road signs and should not continue onto the railway if your vehicle touches any height barrier or bells.

The available clearance is usually 5 metres (16 feet 6 inches), but it may be lower.

Laws: RTA 1988 Section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 2, Part 7.

Rule 293

Controlled crossings

Most controlled crossings have traffic-light signals with a steady amber light, twin flashing red stop lights (see ‘Light signals controlling traffic’ and ‘Traffic signs’) and an audible alarm for pedestrians. They may have full barriers, half-barriers or no barriers.

• You MUST always obey the flashing red stop lights
• You MUST stop behind the white line across the road
• keep going if you have already crossed the white line when the amber light comes on
• do not reverse onto or over a controlled crossing
• you MUST wait if a train passes and the red lights continue to flash, as another train will be passing soon
• cross only when the lights go off and the barriers open
• never zig-zag around half-barriers; they lower automatically because a train is approaching
• at crossings without barriers, a train is approaching when the lights show.

Laws: RTA 1988 Section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 14, Parts 1 and 4.

Rule 294

Railway telephones

If you are driving a large or slow-moving vehicle, a long, low vehicle that risks grounding, or are herding animals, a train could arrive before you are clear of the crossing.

You MUST obey any sign instructing you to use the railway telephone to obtain permission to cross. You MUST also telephone when clear of the crossing if requested to do so.

Laws: RTA 1988 Section 36 and TSRGD Schedule 9, Parts 7 and 8.

Rule 295

Crossings without traffic lights

Vehicles should stop and wait at the barrier or gate when it begins to close. Do not cross until the barrier or gate opens.

Rule 296

User-operated gates or barriers

Some crossings have ‘Stop’ signs and small red and green lights. You MUST NOT cross when the red light is showing; cross only when the green light is on.

If crossing with a vehicle, you should:

• open the gates or barriers on both sides of the crossing
• check that the green light is still on and cross quickly
• close the gates or barriers when you are clear of the crossing.

Laws: TWA 1992 Section 55 and PC(SB)R 1996.

Rule 297

If there are no lights, follow the procedure in Rule 296. Stop, look both ways and listen before crossing.

If there is a railway telephone, always use it to contact the signal operator and make sure it is safe to cross. Inform the signal operator again when you are clear of the crossing.

Rule 298

Open crossings

Open crossings have no gates, barriers, attendant or traffic lights, but they have a ‘Give Way’ sign. Look both ways, listen and make sure that no train is coming before crossing.

Rule 299

Incidents and breakdowns

If your vehicle breaks down or you have an incident on a crossing, you should:

• get everyone out of the vehicle and clear of the crossing immediately
• use a railway telephone, if available, to tell the signal operator and follow the instructions given
• move the vehicle clear of the crossing if there is time before a train arrives
• if the alarm sounds or the amber light comes on, leave the vehicle and get clear of the crossing immediately.

category: The Highway Code. 15. Road works, level crossings and tramways (288 to 307)
description:
Tramways (Rules 300 to 307)

Rule 300

You MUST NOT enter a road, lane or other route reserved for trams. Take extra care where trams run along the road.

Avoid driving directly on top of the rails. Take care where trams leave the main carriageway to enter a reserved route, and make sure that you do not follow them.

The width used by trams is often shown by tram lanes marked with white lines, yellow dots or a different type of road surface.

Diamond-shaped signs and white light signals give instructions to tram drivers only.

Law: RTRA Sections 5 and 8.

Rule 301

Take extra care where the track crosses from one side of the road to the other, and where the road narrows and the tracks come close to the kerb.

Tram drivers usually have their own traffic signals and may be permitted to move when you are not.

Always give way to trams. Do not try to race or overtake them or pass them on the inside unless they are at a tram stop or stopped by tram signals and there is a designated tram lane for you to pass.

Rule 302

You MUST NOT park where your vehicle would obstruct trams or force other drivers to obstruct them.

Do not stop on any part of a tram track, except in a designated bay provided alongside and clear of the track. When using such a bay, ensure that every part of your vehicle is outside the delineated tram path.

Remember that a tram cannot steer around an obstruction.

Law: RTRA Sections 5 and 8.

Rule 303

Tram stops

Where a tram stops at a platform in the middle or at the side of the road, you MUST follow the route shown by road signs and markings.

At stops without platforms, you MUST NOT drive between a tram and the left-hand kerb when the tram has stopped to pick up passengers.

If no alternative route is signed, do not overtake the tram. Wait until it moves off.

Law: RTRA Sections 5 and 8.

Rule 304

Look out for pedestrians, especially children, running to catch a tram approaching a stop.

Rule 305

Always give priority to trams, especially when they signal to pull away from stops, unless it would be unsafe to do so.

Remember that trams may carry large numbers of standing passengers who could be injured if the tram had to make an emergency stop.

Look out for people getting off a bus or tram and crossing the road.

Rule 306

All road users, particularly cyclists and motorcyclists, should take extra care when travelling close to or crossing tram tracks, especially when the rails are wet.

Take particular care when crossing rails at shallow angles, on bends and at junctions. It is safest to cross the tracks directly at right angles.

Other road users should be aware that cyclists and motorcyclists may need more space to cross the tracks safely.

Rule 307

Overhead electric lines

Tramway overhead wires are normally 5.8 metres above the carriageway but may be lower. Before driving beneath an overhead wire, ensure that there is sufficient clearance for your vehicle, including any load it is carrying.

Drivers of vehicles with extending cranes, booms, tipping apparatus or other variable-height equipment should ensure that the equipment is fully lowered.

Where overhead wires are lower than 5.8 metres, height-clearance markings similar to ‘low bridge’ signs will be displayed. Carefully note and obey the clearances shown on these plates.

If you are unsure whether your vehicle can pass safely beneath the wires, contact the local police or tramway operator. Never take a chance, as doing so can be extremely hazardous.

category: The Highway Code. 16. Light signals controlling traffic
subcategory: Traffic light signals. Flashing red lights. Lane control signals
englishSubcategory: Traffic light signals. Flashing red lights. Lane control signals
description:
Traffic light signals

RED means ‘Stop’. Wait behind the stop line on the carriageway.

RED AND AMBER also means ‘Stop’. Do not pass through or start until GREEN shows.

GREEN means that you may proceed if the way is clear. Take special care if you intend to turn left or right, and give way to pedestrians who are crossing.

AMBER means ‘Stop’ at the stop line. You may proceed only if AMBER appears after you have crossed the stop line or when you are so close to it that stopping might cause an accident.

A GREEN ARROW may be provided in addition to the full green signal if movement in a particular direction is allowed before or after the full green phase. If the way is clear, you may proceed only in the direction shown by the arrow. You may do this regardless of which other lights are showing.

White light signals may be provided for trams.

Flashing red lights

Alternately flashing red lights mean YOU MUST STOP. These may be used at level crossings, lifting bridges, airfields, fire stations and other locations.

Lane control signals

• green arrow: the lane is available to traffic facing the sign
• red crosses: the lane is closed to traffic facing the sign
• white diagonal arrow: change lanes in the direction shown.

category: The Highway Code. 16. Light signals controlling traffic
description:
Motorway signals

These signals are also used on other high-speed roads.

Red flashing lights and a red ‘X’

You MUST NOT proceed further in the lane beneath a red ‘X’. The lane is closed.

White diagonal arrow

Change lanes in the direction shown by the arrow.

Reduced visibility ahead

A signal displaying ‘Fog’ warns of reduced visibility ahead.

Lane ahead closed

A diagram showing a lane ending warns that the lane ahead is closed and indicates the direction in which traffic should move.

Temporary maximum speed advised and information message

A speed displayed without a red circle, accompanied by flashing amber lights, advises a temporary maximum speed. A message such as ‘ACCIDENT AHEAD’ may explain the hazard.

Closed lane, temporary mandatory maximum speed limit and information message

A red ‘X’ means that you MUST NOT enter or proceed in the lane beneath it. Arrows indicate the lanes that remain open. A speed displayed within a red circle is a temporary mandatory maximum speed limit. An information message, such as ‘Obstruction’, may identify the hazard.

Temporary maximum speed advised

A speed displayed without a red circle and accompanied by flashing amber lights is an advised temporary maximum speed.

End of restriction

A signal displaying ‘End’ indicates the end of the restriction.

category: The Highway Code. 17. Signals to other road users
subcategory: Direction indicator signals. Brake light signals. Reversing light signals. Arm signals. Hazard lights
englishSubcategory: Direction indicator signals. Brake light signals. Reversing light signals. Arm signals. Hazard lights
description:
Direction indicator signals

• a right direction indicator means: ‘I intend to move out to the right or turn right’
• a left direction indicator means: ‘I intend to move in to the left, turn left or stop on the left’.

These signals should not be used except for the purposes described.

Brake light signals

Illuminated brake lights mean: ‘I am applying the brakes’.

This signal should not be used except for the purpose described.

Reversing light signals

An illuminated white reversing light means: ‘I intend to reverse’.

This signal should not be used except for the purpose described.

Arm signals

Arm signals may be used when direction indicators are not used or when necessary to reinforce direction indicator signals and stop lights. They may also be used by pedal cyclists and people in charge of horses.

Arm signals can indicate:

• ‘I intend to move in to the left or turn left’
• ‘I intend to move out to the right or turn right’
• ‘I intend to slow down or stop’.

The illustrations show a driver using the right arm to signal right, left or slowing down and stopping. They also show a rider extending an arm to the left or right to indicate the intended direction, and moving an arm up and down to indicate slowing down or stopping.

These signals should not be used except for the purposes described.

Hazard lights

Hazard warning lights mean: ‘I am temporarily obstructing traffic or warning of a hazard or obstruction ahead’ (see Rule 116). Both direction indicators flash together when the hazard warning lights are operating.

category: The Highway Code. 18. Signals by authorised persons
subcategory: Police officers. Arm signals to persons controlling traffic. Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency officers and traffic officers. School crossing patrols
englishSubcategory: Police officers. Arm signals to persons controlling traffic. Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency officers and traffic officers. School crossing patrols
description:
Police officers

Stop signals may be directed to:

• traffic approaching from the front
• traffic approaching from both the front and behind
• traffic approaching from behind.

A police officer may signal traffic to stop by facing the relevant traffic and holding up a hand with the palm facing it. An officer may stop traffic approaching from the front and behind by extending the arms as illustrated.

To beckon traffic on, a police officer may signal:

• from the side
• from the front
• from behind.

The officer uses a repeated hand or arm movement to beckon the traffic forward.

In Wales, bilingual signs appear on emergency-services vehicles and clothing.

Arm signals to people controlling traffic

Drivers may use arm signals to communicate:

• ‘I want to go straight on’
• ‘I want to turn left’; either hand may be used
• ‘I want to turn right’.

Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency officers and traffic officers

Traffic officers and DVSA officers have powers to stop or direct vehicles. They use hand signals and light signals similar to those used by the police. You MUST obey any signals they give (see Rules 107 and 108).

School crossing patrols

The position of the patrol sign indicates:

• sign held vertically with the sign face down: not ready to cross pedestrians
• sign held horizontally across the road: a barrier to stop pedestrians crossing
• sign raised diagonally with the sign visible: ready to cross pedestrians; vehicles must be prepared to stop
• sign held upright and displayed towards traffic, with the patrol officer’s other arm extended: all vehicles must stop.

category: The Highway Code. 19. Traffic signs
description:
Signs giving orders

Signs with red circles are mostly prohibitive. Plates below signs qualify their message.

Prohibitory and restriction signs

• entry to a 20 mph zone
• end of a 20 mph zone
• maximum speed; the illustration shows 40 mph as an example
• national speed limit applies
• school crossing patrol
• STOP and give way
• give way to traffic on the major road
• manually operated temporary STOP and GO signs
• no entry for vehicular traffic
• no vehicles except bicycles being pushed
• no cycling
• no motor vehicles
• no buses with more than eight passenger seats
• no overtaking
• no towed caravans
• no vehicles carrying explosives
• no vehicle or combination of vehicles over the length shown; the illustration includes examples of 32 feet 6 inches and 9.9 metres
• no vehicles over the height shown; the illustration shows 4.4 metres or 14 feet 6 inches
• no vehicles over the width shown; the illustration shows 2.0 metres or 6 feet 6 inches
• give priority to vehicles from the opposite direction
• no right turn
• no left turn
• no U-turns
• no goods vehicles over the maximum gross weight shown, in tonnes, except for loading and unloading; the illustration shows 7.5 tonnes
• no vehicles over the maximum gross weight shown, in tonnes; the illustration shows a weak-bridge restriction of 18 tonnes maximum gross weight
• parking restricted to permit holders
• no stopping during the indicated period except for buses
• no stopping during the times shown except for as long as necessary to set down or pick up passengers. The illustrated urban-clearway example applies Monday to Friday from 8:00 am to 9:30 am and from 4:30 pm to 6:30 pm
• no waiting
• no stopping or clearway.

Signs with blue circles but no red border mostly give positive instructions.

Positive instruction signs

• ahead only
• turn left ahead; turn right if the symbol is reversed
• turn left; turn right if the symbol is reversed
• keep left; keep right if the symbol is reversed
• vehicles may pass either side to reach the same destination
• mini-roundabout: follow roundabout circulation and give way to vehicles from the immediate right
• route for pedal cycles only
• segregated pedal-cycle and pedestrian route
• minimum speed; the illustration shows 30 mph as an example
• end of minimum speed
• buses and cycles only
• trams only
• pedestrian crossing point over a tramway; look both ways
• one-way traffic; compare this rectangular sign with the circular ‘Ahead only’ sign
• with-flow bus and cycle lane
• contra-flow bus lane
• with-flow pedal-cycle lane.

category: The Highway Code. 19. Traffic signs
description:
Warning signs

Warning signs are mostly triangular with red borders. A plate beneath a warning sign may provide extra information, such as the distance to or length of the hazard.

Junction, road-layout and traffic warnings

• distance to a ‘STOP’ line ahead; the illustration shows 100 yards
• dual carriageway ends
• road narrows on the right; the symbol is reversed when the road narrows on the left
• road narrows on both sides
• distance to a ‘Give Way’ line ahead; the illustration shows 50 yards
• crossroads
• junction on a bend ahead
• T-junction with priority over vehicles approaching from the right
• staggered junction
• traffic merging from the left ahead
• the priority through route is indicated by the broader line
• double bend, first to the left; the symbol may be reversed
• bend to the right; the symbol is reversed for a bend to the left
• roundabout
• two-way traffic crosses a one-way road
• two-way traffic straight ahead
• traffic signals
• traffic signals not in use
• traffic queues likely ahead
• sharp deviation of the route to the left; the chevrons are reversed for a deviation to the right
• worded warnings, including ‘REDUCE SPEED NOW’.

Road-condition and environmental warnings

• uneven road
• slippery road
• steep hill downwards
• steep hill upwards
• gradients may be shown as a percentage or ratio; for example, 20% equals 1:5. The illustration also shows a 10% downward gradient and a 20% upward gradient
• tunnel ahead
• falling or fallen rocks
• risk of ice; a plate may state ‘Ice’
• distance over which road humps extend; the illustration shows ‘Humps for 2 miles’
• other danger; a plate indicates the nature of the danger
• soft verges; the illustration shows ‘Soft verges for 2 miles’
• side winds
• hump bridge
• quayside or river bank
• risk of grounding
• a worded plate may identify hazards such as a hidden dip or ford.

Railway, tramway, bridge and aircraft warnings

• opening or swing bridge ahead
• low-flying aircraft or sudden aircraft noise
• trams crossing ahead
• level crossing with a barrier or gate ahead
• level crossing without a barrier or gate ahead
• level crossing without a barrier, shown by a crossbuck sign
• light signals ahead at a level crossing, airfield or bridge
• miniature warning lights at level crossings. Red means ‘STOP’, green means ‘Clear’, and if no light shows, telephone the crossing operator
• alternately flashing red lights mean stop when the lights show.

Pedestrian and crossing warnings

• school crossing patrol ahead; some signs have amber lights that flash when the crossing is in use
• frail pedestrians likely to cross; blind or disabled pedestrians may be shown instead
• pedestrians in the road ahead; a plate may indicate that there is no footway for a stated distance, shown as 400 yards in the illustration
• zebra crossing.

Height and electrical warnings

• overhead electric cable; the plate indicates the maximum vehicle height that can pass safely. The illustration shows a safe height of 16 feet 6 inches or 5.0 metres
• available headroom indicated; the illustration shows 14 feet 6 inches or 4.4 metres.

Animal and cycle warnings

• cattle
• wild animals
• wild horses or ponies
• accompanied horses or ponies
• cycle route ahead.

category: The Highway Code. 19. Traffic signs
description:
Direction signs

Direction signs are mostly rectangular.

Signs on motorways

Motorway direction signs have blue backgrounds.

• a sign at a junction leading directly into a motorway may show the junction number on a black background
• signs on approaches to motorway junctions may show the junction number on a black background
• a route-confirmatory sign after a junction lists destinations and distances
• downward-pointing arrows mean ‘Get in lane’. They may show that the left-hand lane leads to a different destination from the other lanes
• a panel with an inclined arrow indicates destinations that can be reached by leaving the motorway at the next junction.

The illustrations include examples for the M1, junction numbers 23 and 25, and route-confirmatory distances of 32 miles to Sheffield and 59 miles to Leeds.

Signs on primary routes

Primary-route signs have green backgrounds.

• blue panels indicate that a motorway starts at the junction ahead
• a motorway shown in brackets can also be reached by following the indicated route
• white panels indicate local or non-primary routes leading from the junction ahead
• brown panels show routes to tourist attractions
• the junction name may appear at the top of the sign
• an aircraft symbol indicates the route to an airport
• a symbol may warn of a hazard or restriction along the route.

Primary-route signs may be placed on approaches to junctions, at junctions and after junctions as route-confirmatory signs. The illustration includes a route warning of a 4.4-metre (14-foot-6-inch) height restriction one mile ahead.

Signs on approaches to junctions in Wales may be bilingual.

A primary route forming part of a ring road is shown by green direction signs with ‘Ring road’ panels. A green square containing a white ‘R’ also indicates a ring-road route.

Signs on non-primary and local routes

These signs have black borders.

• green panels indicate that a primary route starts at the junction ahead
• route numbers on a blue background show the direction to a motorway
• route numbers on a green background show the direction to a primary route
• signs may be provided on approaches to junctions and at junctions
• a sign showing ‘WC’ and a wheelchair symbol gives the direction to toilets with access for disabled people.

Other direction signs

• picnic site
• ancient monument in the care of English Heritage
• direction to a car park; a qualifying panel may limit its availability, such as ‘Saturday only’
• tourist attraction; brown signs are used, with examples including a zoo
• direction to a camping and caravan site; the illustration shows one 300 yards away
• advisory route for lorries
• route for pedal cycles forming part of a network; a red route-number patch may identify the numbered route, such as route 4
• recommended route for pedal cycles to the place shown; the illustration shows Marton three miles away
• route for pedestrians; examples include directions to a public library or council offices
• symbols showing an emergency diversion route for motorway and other main-road traffic. The symbols shown are a square, triangle, circle and diamond on yellow backgrounds
• a temporary diversion route is shown by a black symbol or destination on a yellow sign.

category: The Highway Code. 19. Traffic signs
description:
Information signs

Information signs are rectangular.

Parking, charging and restriction information

• entrance to a controlled parking zone. The illustrated example operates Monday to Friday from 8:30 am to 6:30 pm and Saturday from 8:30 am to 1:30 pm
• entrance to a congestion-charging zone. The illustrated Central Zone example operates Monday to Friday from 7:00 am to 6:30 pm
• end of a controlled parking zone
• advance warning of a restriction or prohibition ahead. The illustrated example warns of a low bridge two miles ahead with a maximum height of 4.4 metres or 14 feet 6 inches
• parking place for solo motorcycles.

Bus lanes and high-occupancy vehicle lanes

• with-flow bus lane ahead that pedal cycles and taxis may also use
• lane designated for high-occupancy vehicles (HOVs); see Rule 142. The illustrated example is for vehicles carrying two or more people and operates Monday to Friday from 7:00 am to 9:00 am and 4:00 pm to 6:00 pm
• signs show which vehicles may use an HOV lane ahead. The illustrated example permits vehicles with two or more people, buses, motorcycles and pedal cycles, but prohibits goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes
• bus lane on the road at the junction ahead. An ‘Except buses’ panel may show that buses are exempt from a directional restriction.

Motorway information

• end of motorway
• start of motorway and the point from which motorway regulations apply; the illustration shows the M62
• appropriate traffic lanes at a junction ahead
• traffic on the main carriageway coming from the right has priority over joining traffic
• additional traffic joins from the left ahead; traffic on the main carriageway has priority over traffic joining from the right-hand lane of the slip road
• traffic in the right-hand lane of the slip road joining the main carriageway has priority over traffic in the left-hand lane
• variable speed limit with camera enforcement.

Countdown markers

At a motorway exit, each bar on a countdown marker represents 100 yards to the exit. Three bars indicate 300 yards, two bars indicate 200 yards and one bar indicates 100 yards.

Green-backed countdown markers may be used on primary routes. White-backed markers with black bars may be used on other routes.

White-backed markers with red bars may be used on approaches to concealed level crossings. Although these markers are placed at equal distances, their bars do not represent intervals of 100 yards.

Other information signs

• motorway service-area sign showing the operator’s name. The illustrated example shows Puddleworth services half a mile ahead and symbols for LPG, refreshments, food, disabled facilities, information, accommodation and petrol
• traffic has priority over oncoming vehicles
• hospital ahead with Accident and Emergency facilities. The illustrated example states that A&E is not open 24 hours
• tourist information point
• no through road for vehicles
• recommended route for pedal cycles
• Home Zone entrance
• area in which cameras are used to enforce traffic regulations.

category: The Highway Code. 19. Traffic signs
description:
Road work signs

• road works
• loose chippings
• temporary hazard at road works. The illustration includes the worded warning ‘SLOW WET TAR’
• temporary lane closure. The number and position of arrows and red bars may vary according to which lanes are open and closed. The illustrated example gives 800 yards’ warning
• slow-moving or stationary works vehicle blocking a traffic lane. Pass in the direction shown by the arrow; the illustrated sign directs traffic to pass on the left
• road works one mile ahead. A supplementary message may provide further information, such as ‘Delays possible until Mar 08’
• mandatory speed limit ahead. The illustration warns of a 50 mph limit three-quarters of a mile ahead
• advance sign combining a road-works warning and temporary lane closure; the illustrated example gives 800 yards’ warning
• end of road works and all temporary restrictions, including temporary speed limits. The illustration includes the message ‘Sorry for any delay’
• signs displayed on the back of slow-moving or stationary vehicles warning that a works vehicle is closing a lane ahead. There are no cones on the road. The illustrated example gives 450 yards’ warning
• lane restrictions at road works ahead. The illustrated example shows restrictions 800 yards ahead for the M1 and A617 at junction 29, including lane destinations and a restriction for vehicles over 7.5 tonnes
• one-lane crossover at contraflow road works. The illustrated sign instructs drivers to stay in lane and shows a maximum speed of 30 mph.

category: The Highway Code. 20. Road markings
subcategory: Across the carriageway. Along the carriageway. Along the edge of the carriageway. On the kerb or at the edge of the carriageway. Other road markings
englishSubcategory: Across the carriageway. Along the carriageway. Along the edge of the carriageway. On the kerb or at the edge of the carriageway. Other road markings
description:
Across the carriageway

• stop line at traffic signals or police control
• stop line at a ‘Stop’ sign
• stop line for pedestrians at a level crossing
• give way to traffic on the major road; this marking may also be used at mini-roundabouts
• give way to traffic approaching from the right at a roundabout
• give way to traffic approaching from the right at a mini-roundabout.

Along the carriageway

• edge line
• centre line; see Rule 127
• hazard warning line; see Rule 127
• double white lines; see Rules 128 and 129
• double white-line system ending; see Rule 130
• lane line; see Rule 131.

Along the edge of the carriageway

Waiting restrictions

Yellow waiting-restriction lines apply to the carriageway, pavement and verge. You may stop to load or unload, unless loading restrictions also apply, or while passengers board or alight.

Double yellow lines mean no waiting at any time unless signs specifically indicate seasonal restrictions. A single yellow line means no waiting during the times shown on a nearby sign or on the entry signs to a controlled parking zone.

If no days are displayed, the restriction applies every day, including Sundays and Bank Holidays. White bay markings and upright signs show where parking is permitted and may specify its permitted duration, days and times.

Red Route stopping controls

Some roads use red lines instead of yellow lines. Single and double red lines prohibit stopping to park, load or unload, or allow passengers to board or alight, subject to stated exceptions for licensed taxis and Blue Badge holders. The restrictions apply to the carriageway, pavement and verge.

Double red lines mean no stopping at any time. Single red lines mean no stopping during the times shown on nearby signs.

On Red Routes, stopping to park or load may be allowed in specially marked bays. A red bay is available only for the stated purpose during the times shown, which may be only part of the day. A white bay is available throughout the day, subject to its sign.

Red and single yellow lines provide only a guide to the restrictions in force. Always consult nearby signs or zone-entry signs.

The illustrated Red Route examples show:

• no stopping at any time
• no stopping Monday to Saturday from 7 am to 7 pm
• parking Monday to Saturday from 7 am to 7 pm for up to one hour, with no return within two hours
• loading between 10 am and 4 pm for up to 20 minutes
• parking Monday to Saturday from 8 am to 7 pm for up to 20 minutes, with no return within 40 minutes.

On the kerb or at the edge of the carriageway

Loading restrictions on roads other than Red Routes

Yellow marks on the kerb or at the edge of the carriageway prohibit loading and unloading during the times shown on nearby black-and-white plates. You may stop while passengers board or alight.

Double yellow kerb marks mean no loading or unloading at any time. A single yellow kerb mark means no loading or unloading during the times shown. If no days are displayed, the restriction applies every day, including Sundays and Bank Holidays. Always check the times shown on the plates.

A loading bay is marked by a white bay with the words ‘Loading Only’ and an upright sign displaying a white-on-blue trolley symbol. The sign states whether the bay is restricted to goods vehicles and when it may be used. If no days or times are displayed, it may be used at any time. A vehicle must not park there unless it is being loaded or unloaded.

Other road markings

• school entrance marking: keep the entrance clear of stationary vehicles, even when picking up or setting down children
• elongated warning triangle: warning of a ‘Give Way’ marking just ahead
• parking bays reserved for the vehicles named, such as doctors; see Rule 243
• bus-stop clearway marking; see Rule 243
• bus-lane marking; see Rule 141
• yellow box junction; see Rule 174
• ‘Keep Clear’ marking: do not block the indicated part of the carriageway
• arrows and destination markings indicate the lanes to use.

category: The Highway Code. 21. Vehicle markings
subcategory: Large goods vehicle rear markings. Hazard warning plates. Projections markers. Other
englishSubcategory: Large goods vehicle rear markings. Hazard warning plates. Projections markers. Other
description:
Large goods vehicle rear markings

Rear markings must be displayed on motor vehicles with a maximum gross weight exceeding 7,500 kilograms and trailers with a maximum gross weight exceeding 3,500 kilograms.

The markings use fluorescent yellow and retroreflective red stripes. They may be arranged as a full-width central marking, two horizontal markings positioned on the left and right, or vertical markings positioned on the left and right.

Vertical red-and-yellow markings must also be fitted to builders’ skips placed in the road and to commercial vehicles or vehicle combinations longer than 13 metres. They are optional on combinations between 11 and 13 metres long.

Hazard warning plates

Certain tank vehicles carrying dangerous goods must display hazard-information panels. The illustrated panel is for a flammable liquid and includes:

• the emergency action code ‘2YE’
• the United Nations substance number ‘1089’
• a flammable-liquid hazard diamond
• a telephone number for specialist advice.

A plain orange panel is displayed by vehicles carrying certain dangerous goods in packages.

Diamond-shaped warning symbols identify particular hazards. The illustrated symbols indicate:

• toxic substance, class 6
• oxidizing substance, class 5.1
• non-flammable compressed gas, class 2
• radioactive substance, class 7
• spontaneously combustible substance, class 4
• corrosive substance, class 8.

Projections markers

Side and end projection markers warn other road users about an overhanging load or projecting equipment, such as a crane jib.

Both side and end markers are required when a load or equipment projects more than two metres beyond the front or rear of a vehicle.

Other

A yellow square sign showing two children identifies a school bus. It may be displayed in the front or rear window of a bus or coach.

category: The Highway Code. 22. Annex 1. You and your bicycle
description:
You and your bicycle

Before riding on the road, make sure that you feel confident in your ability to ride safely.

Choosing and maintaining your cycle

Make sure that:

• you have the correct size and type of cycle for your comfort and safety
• the lights and reflectors are clean and in good working order
• the tyres are in good condition and inflated to the pressure shown on the tyre
• the wheels spin freely
• the gears work correctly
• the chain is properly adjusted and oiled
• the saddle and handlebars are adjusted to the correct height.

You should fit a bell to your cycle.

Legal requirements

You MUST:

• ensure that your brakes are efficient
• have a white front light and a red rear light lit when cycling at night.

Laws PCUR regulations 6 and 10 and RVLR regulation 18.

Cycle training

If you are an inexperienced cyclist or have not ridden for some time, consider taking a cycle-training course. Some councils provide national-standard training such as Bikeability, and it is free of charge in certain areas. Training can help develop your cycling skills and confidence.

Bikeability has three levels. It begins with basic skills such as balancing, stopping and starting safely and progresses to handling complex and busy junctions.

Training may also cover:

• traffic signs and the rules of the road
• route planning
• safe road positioning
• signalling, particularly at junctions
• basic cycle maintenance.

Further information is available from www.bikeability.org.uk and www.cycling.scot.

category: The Highway Code. 23. Annex 2. Motorcycle licence requirements
subcategory: Motorcycle licence requirements. Licence categories for mopeds and motorcycles
englishSubcategory: Motorcycle licence requirements. Licence categories for mopeds and motorcycles
description:
Motorcycle licence requirements

If you hold a provisional motorcycle licence, you MUST satisfactorily complete a Compulsory Basic Training (CBT) course.

After completing CBT, you may ride unaccompanied on a public road for up to two years on a motorcycle that:

• has an engine capacity of no more than 125 cc
• has a power output not exceeding 11 kW
• displays L plates. In Wales, D plates, L plates or both may be used.

Law RTA 1988 section 97(3).

Learning to ride a moped

To ride a moped as a learner, you MUST:

• be at least 16 years old
• hold a provisional moped licence
• complete CBT.

Law RTA 1988 sections 97(3) and 101.

You may then ride unaccompanied on a public road for up to two years on a two-wheeled vehicle with a maximum design speed of 45 km/h (28 mph), provided that you display L plates. In Wales, D plates, L plates or both may be used.

To obtain a full moped licence, you MUST first pass the motorcycle theory test and then the moped practical test.

Law MV(DL)R regulation 38(4).

Drivers who passed the car test before 1 February 2001

If you passed your car driving test before 1 February 2001, you are qualified to ride a moped without L plates or, in Wales, D plates. However, completing CBT before riding on the road is recommended.

If you passed your car driving test on or after 1 February 2001, you MUST complete CBT before riding a moped on the road.

Law RTA 1988 section 97(3).

Licence categories for mopeds and motorcycles

Category AM — minimum age 16

• a two-wheeled vehicle with a maximum design speed of 45 km/h (28 mph)
• a three- or four-wheeled vehicle with a maximum design speed exceeding 25 km/h (15.5 mph), an engine capacity of no more than 50 cc and a power output not exceeding 4 kW.

Category A1 — minimum age 17

• motorcycles with an engine capacity of no more than 125 cc and a power output not exceeding 11 kW
• tricycles with a power output not exceeding 15 kW.

Category A2 — minimum age 19

• motorcycles with a power output not exceeding 35 kW.

Category A

• any motorcycle. The minimum age is 21 through progressive access or 24 through direct access
• tricycles with a power output exceeding 15 kW; the minimum age is 21.

Progressive access

Progressive access allows a rider to take the practical test for a higher licence category after gaining at least two years’ experience in a lower motorcycle category.

For example, a rider who has held a category A2 licence for at least two years may take the category A practical test at age 21. Another theory test is not required.

Learning on a motorcycle larger than 125 cc

To learn to ride a motorcycle with an engine capacity over 125 cc and a power output over 11 kW, you MUST:

• meet the applicable minimum-age requirements
• satisfactorily complete CBT
• be accompanied by an approved instructor riding another motorcycle and maintaining radio contact.

Law MV(DL)R regulations 9 and 16(7), and RTA 1988 section 97(3).

Obtaining a full licence

To obtain a full moped or motorcycle licence, you MUST pass:

• the motorcycle theory test
• the Module 1 practical test
• the Module 2 practical test.

The practical tests must be taken on a two-wheeled motorcycle.

Law MV(DL)R regulation 38.

Until you have passed your test, you MUST NOT:

• carry a pillion passenger
• pull a trailer.

Also see Rule 253 concerning vehicles prohibited from motorways.

Law MV(DL)R regulation 16.

category: The Highway Code. 24. Annex 3. Motor vehicle documentation and learner driver requirements
description:
Documents

Driving licence

You MUST hold a valid driving licence for the category of motor vehicle you are driving. You MUST notify the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA) if your name or address changes.

Law RTA 1988 sections 87 and 99(4).

Non-European Community licences

A holder of a non-European Community licence who becomes resident in the UK may drive using that licence for a maximum of 12 months from the date they become resident.

To maintain continuous entitlement to drive, the driver should, before the 12-month period expires, either:

• obtain a British provisional licence and pass the required driving test or tests
• exchange an eligible licence for a British licence if it was issued by a country designated in law for licence-exchange purposes.

MOT

Cars and motorcycles MUST normally pass their first MOT test three years after their initial registration and every year thereafter.

You MUST NOT drive a motor vehicle without an MOT certificate when one is required. Exceptions allow you to drive to a pre-arranged MOT appointment or to a garage for repairs required for the test. Driving an unroadworthy vehicle may invalidate your insurance.

Cars, vans, motorcycles and other light passenger vehicles manufactured or first registered more than 40 years ago are exempt from MOT testing unless they have been substantially changed within the previous 30 years. Guidance about substantial changes is available at www.gov.uk/historic-vehicles.

If an MOT-exempt vehicle is substantially changed, its keeper cannot continue claiming the exemption.

Law RTA 1988 sections 45, 47, 49 and 53.

Insurance

To use a motor vehicle on the road, you MUST have a valid insurance policy. It MUST provide at least third-party cover for injury to another person or damage to another person’s property.

Before driving any motor vehicle, make sure that either the vehicle’s policy covers you or your own insurance provides adequate cover. You MUST NOT drive without insurance. Even when a road traffic incident is not your fault, an insurance company may still hold you liable.

Law RTA 1988 section 143.

Roadside cameras can automatically detect uninsured vehicles. In addition to other penalties, the police may seize, remove and crush an uninsured offender’s vehicle.

Law RTA 1988 sections 165A and 165B.

Types of insurance

Third-party insurance is often the cheapest type and is the minimum cover required by law. It covers injury caused to other people and damage caused to their property. It does not cover damage to your own vehicle or personal injury to you.

Third-party, fire and theft insurance provides third-party cover and also covers your vehicle if it is stolen or damaged by fire.

Comprehensive insurance provides third-party cover and also covers damage to your own vehicle, up to its market value, and personal injury to you. It is generally the most extensive and most expensive type of cover.

Registration certificate

Registration certificates, also called harmonised registration certificates, are issued for motor vehicles used on the road. They describe the vehicle, including its make and model, and identify its registered keeper.

You MUST notify the DVLA in Swansea as soon as possible when you buy or sell a motor vehicle or change your name or address.

The buyer and seller are responsible for completing the registration certificate. The seller is responsible for forwarding it to the DVLA. The procedures are explained on the back of the certificate.

Law RV(R&L)R regulations 21, 22, 23 and 24.

Vehicle Excise Duty

Vehicle Excise Duty (VED) MUST be paid for every motor vehicle used or kept on a public road.

Law VERA sections 29 and 33.

Statutory Off-Road Notification

A Statutory Off-Road Notification (SORN) informs the DVLA that a motor vehicle is not being used on the road.

If you are the registered keeper and intend to keep a vehicle untaxed and off the public road, you MUST declare SORN. Failing to do so is an offence. The SORN remains in force until the vehicle is sold, taxed or scrapped.

An unused vehicle or one kept off the road MUST have either a SORN declaration or valid insurance.

Law RV(RL)R regulation 26 and Schedule 4.

Production of documents

When requested by a police officer, you MUST be able to produce:

• your driving licence
• a valid insurance certificate
• a valid MOT certificate, when applicable.

If you cannot produce the documents immediately, you may be required to take them to a police station within seven days.

Law RTA 1988 sections 164 and 165.

Learner drivers

A learner driving a car MUST hold a valid provisional licence.

The learner MUST be supervised by someone who:

• is at least 21 years old
• holds a full EC or EEA licence for the relevant type of car, whether automatic or manual
• has held that licence for at least three years.

Laws MV(DL)R regulation 16 and RTA 1988 section 87.

Learner vehicles

A vehicle being driven by a learner MUST display red L plates. In Wales, red D plates, red L plates or both may be used.

The plates MUST comply with legal specifications and be clearly visible to other road users from both the front and rear of the vehicle.

Learner plates should be removed or covered when the vehicle is not being driven by a learner, except on driving-school vehicles.

Law MV(DL)R regulation 16 and Schedule 4.

Driving unaccompanied

Before driving unaccompanied, you MUST pass the theory test, when one is required, followed by the practical driving test for the category of vehicle you wish to drive.

Law MV(DL)R regulation 40.

description:
Road traffic law

The Acts and Regulations listed below are abbreviated throughout the Highway Code. This is not a comprehensive guide to road traffic law. For the precise wording, refer to the relevant legislation, including any amendments.

Application and meaning of ‘road’

Most provisions apply on all roads throughout Great Britain, although exceptions exist.

In England and Wales, a road is defined as ‘any highway and any other road to which the public has access and includes bridges over which a road passes’; see RTA 1988 section 192(1).

Scotland has a similar definition, extended to include any way over which the public has a right of passage; see R(S)A 1984 section 151(1).

References to a road therefore generally include:

• footpaths
• bridleways
• cycle tracks
• many roads and driveways on private land
• many car parks.

Road traffic law usually applies in these places, although additional rules may govern particular paths or ways. Some serious offences, including drink-driving offences, apply in all public places, such as public car parks.

Emergency areas

An ‘emergency area’ in the Highway Code means an ‘emergency refuge area’ as defined by the Motorways Traffic (England and Wales) Regulations 1982, as amended by the Motorways Traffic (England and Wales) (Amendment) (England) Regulations 2015.

category: The Highway Code. 26. Annex 5. Penalties
description:
Penalties and the Highway Code

Parliament sets the maximum penalties for road traffic offences. The maximum penalty reflects the seriousness of the offence, but the courts decide the sentence imposed in each case according to the circumstances.

The penalty table lists some of the principal offences and their associated penalties. Many other specific offences are not included.

Penalty points and disqualification

The penalty-point system is intended to deter drivers and motorcyclists from unsafe practices. Certain non-motoring offences, such as failing to rectify vehicle defects, may also attract penalty points.

The court MUST order the number of points fixed by Parliament, or a number within the prescribed range, to be endorsed on the offender’s licence. Accumulated points warn drivers and motorcyclists that further offences may result in disqualification.

Law RTOA sections 44 and 45.

A driver or motorcyclist who accumulates 12 or more penalty points within three years MUST be disqualified for at least six months. The period may be longer if the offender has previously been disqualified.

Law RTOA section 35.

For every offence carrying penalty points, the court has discretion to disqualify the licence holder. The court may select any appropriate period, although it will usually range from one week to several months.

For serious offences such as dangerous driving and drink-driving, the court MUST order disqualification. The minimum period is normally 12 months, but it may be longer for repeat offenders or when the alcohol level is high. A second drink-driving offence within ten years results in disqualification for at least three years.

Law RTOA section 34.

Penalty table

Causing death by dangerous driving

• maximum penalty: life imprisonment and an unlimited fine
• obligatory disqualification for at least five years
• 3 to 11 penalty points if the offender is exceptionally not disqualified.

Dangerous driving

• maximum penalty: two years’ imprisonment and an unlimited fine
• obligatory disqualification
• 3 to 11 penalty points if the offender is exceptionally not disqualified.

Causing death by careless driving while under the influence of drink or drugs

• maximum penalty: life imprisonment and an unlimited fine
• obligatory disqualification for at least five years
• 3 to 11 penalty points if the offender is exceptionally not disqualified.

Careless and inconsiderate driving

• unlimited fine
• discretionary disqualification
• 3 to 9 penalty points.

Driving while unfit through drink or drugs, driving with excess alcohol, or failing to provide a specimen for analysis

• maximum penalty: six months’ imprisonment and an unlimited fine
• obligatory disqualification
• 3 to 11 penalty points if the offender is exceptionally not disqualified.

Failing to stop after an accident or failing to report an accident

• maximum penalty: six months’ imprisonment and an unlimited fine
• discretionary disqualification
• 5 to 10 penalty points.

Driving while disqualified

• maximum penalty: six months’ imprisonment, or 12 months in Scotland, and an unlimited fine
• discretionary disqualification
• 6 penalty points.

Driving after a licence has been refused or revoked on medical grounds

• maximum penalty: six months’ imprisonment and an unlimited fine
• discretionary disqualification
• 3 to 6 penalty points.

Driving without insurance

• unlimited fine
• discretionary disqualification
• 6 to 8 penalty points.

Using a vehicle in a dangerous condition

• unlimited fine for a large goods vehicle or passenger-carrying vehicle
• maximum fine of £2,500 for other vehicles
• obligatory disqualification for at least six months if the offence is committed within three years of a previous conviction for a similar offence; otherwise disqualification is discretionary
• 3 penalty points in each case.

Failing to have proper control of a vehicle or a full view of the road and traffic ahead

• maximum fine of £1,000, or £2,500 when driving a passenger-carrying or goods vehicle
• discretionary disqualification
• 3 penalty points.

Using a hand-held mobile phone while driving

• maximum fine of £1,000, or £2,500 when driving a passenger-carrying or goods vehicle
• discretionary disqualification
• 6 penalty points.

Driving otherwise than in accordance with a licence

• maximum fine of £1,000
• discretionary disqualification
• 3 to 6 penalty points.

Speeding

• maximum fine of £1,000, or £2,500 for a motorway offence
• discretionary disqualification
• 3 to 6 penalty points, or 3 points for a fixed penalty.

Traffic-light offences

• maximum fine of £1,000
• discretionary disqualification
• 3 penalty points.

No MOT certificate

• maximum fine of £1,000
• no penalty points shown in the table.

Seat-belt offences

• maximum fine of £500
• no penalty points shown in the table.

Dangerous cycling

• maximum fine of £2,500
• no penalty points shown in the table.

Careless cycling

• maximum fine of £1,000
• no penalty points shown in the table.

Cycling on the pavement

• maximum fine of £500
• no penalty points shown in the table.

Failing to identify the driver of a vehicle

• maximum fine of £1,000
• discretionary disqualification
• 6 penalty points.

Retesting after disqualification

When a court disqualifies an offender after conviction for an offence marked as requiring an extended retest, it must order that retest.

A court may also order:

• a retest for any other offence carrying penalty points
• an extended retest when disqualification is obligatory
• an ordinary test when disqualification is not obligatory.

In some serious cases, the court MUST impose a fixed period of disqualification and then continue the disqualification until the offender passes a driving test. In other cases, the court has discretion to make such an order. Depending on the offence, the required test may be an ordinary or extended test.

Law RTOA section 36.

New drivers

Special rules apply for two years from the date on which a driver or motorcyclist passes their first driving test. They apply to:

• people from the UK, EU or EEA, Isle of Man, Channel Islands or Gibraltar who passed their first test in any of those places
• drivers from other countries who must pass a UK test to obtain a UK licence; the UK test is treated as their first test
• drivers who exchange a foreign licence for a UK licence without taking a test and later pass a UK test for another vehicle category; that UK test is treated as their first test.

For example, a person who exchanges a foreign car licence for a UK car licence and subsequently passes an HGV test becomes subject to the special rules.

If a new driver accumulates six or more penalty points before the two-year period ends, their licence is revoked automatically. This includes points acquired before they passed the test.

To regain a licence, the person must apply for a new provisional licence and may drive only as a learner until they pass a further driving test. See also Annex 8, Safety code for new drivers.

Law RT(ND)A.

These rules also apply when the points result from offences dealt with by fixed penalties.

A driver in the UK, EU or EEA, Isle of Man, Channel Islands or Gibraltar group who already holds a full licence for one type of vehicle is not subject to the special rules merely because they later pass a test for another vehicle type.

Other consequences of offending

When an offence is punishable by imprisonment, the vehicle used to commit it may be confiscated.

Law SA sections 152, 153, 154 and 155.

A serious driving conviction is also likely to increase the cost of insurance considerably because insurers consider convicted drivers more likely to be involved in a collision.

Before their licence is returned, certain high-risk drink-drive offenders must satisfy the DVLA Medical Branch that they do not have an alcohol problem and are otherwise fit to drive. This applies to drivers who:

• are disqualified for drink-driving twice within ten years
• are disqualified once with an alcohol level more than two-and-a-half times the legal limit
• refuse to provide a specimen.

Persistent misuse of drugs or alcohol may result in the withdrawal of a driving licence.

category: The Highway Code. 27. Annex 6. Vehicle maintenance, safety and security
description:
Vehicle maintenance

Take special care to ensure that the following are working correctly:

• lights
• brakes
• steering
• exhaust system
• seat belts
• demisters
• windscreen wipers and washers
• audible warning systems.

You MUST keep lights, indicators, reflectors and number plates clean and unobstructed.

Windscreens and windows MUST be clean and free from anything that obstructs your view.

Lights MUST be adjusted correctly so that they do not dazzle other road users. Pay particular attention to their adjustment when the vehicle is heavily loaded.

Exhaust emissions MUST NOT exceed the prescribed levels.

Before driving, correctly adjust your seat, seat belt, head restraint and mirrors. Make sure that luggage is securely stowed.

Laws RVLR 1989 regulations 23 and 27, and CUR regulations 30 and 61.

Warning displays

Understand the meaning of every warning display on the instrument panel. Never ignore a warning because it may indicate that a dangerous fault is developing.

Warning lights normally illuminate when the ignition is switched on and go out when the engine starts, except for the handbrake warning light while the handbrake is engaged.

If a warning light does not go out or illuminates while you are driving, stop and investigate because the vehicle may have a serious fault.

A charge warning light appearing while you are driving may mean that the battery is not charging. Have the problem checked as soon as possible to avoid losing power to the lights and other electrical systems.

Window tints

You MUST NOT use a vehicle with excessively dark tinting on the windscreen or either front side window. Tinting applied during manufacture complies with the applicable Visual Light Transmittance (VLT) standards.

There are no VLT limits for the rear windscreen or rear passenger windows.

Laws RTA 1988 section 42 and CUR regulation 32.

Tyres

Tyres MUST be inflated correctly according to the vehicle manufacturer’s specification for the load being carried. Consult the vehicle handbook or technical data. Tyres should be free from prohibited cuts and other defects.

Cars, light vans and light trailers MUST have at least 1.6 mm of tread across the central three-quarters of the tread’s width and around its entire circumference.

Motorcycles, large vehicles and passenger-carrying vehicles MUST have at least 1 mm of tread across three-quarters of the tread’s width and in a continuous band around the entire circumference.

Moped tyres should have visible tread.

Some vehicle defects can result in penalty points.

Tyre age

Tyres more than ten years old MUST NOT be used on the front axles of:

• goods vehicles with a maximum gross weight exceeding 3.5 tonnes
• passenger vehicles with more than eight passenger seats.

They MUST NOT be used on the rear axles of passenger vehicles with 9 to 16 passenger seats unless the axle has twin wheels.

The marking showing a tyre’s manufacture date MUST always be legible so that its age can be established.

Vehicles excluded from tyre-roadworthiness regulations and historic vehicles not used commercially are exempt from these tyre-age requirements.

Law CUR regulation 27.

Tyre failures

If a tyre bursts while you are driving, grip the steering wheel firmly, try to retain control and allow the vehicle to roll to a stop at the side of the road.

If you have a flat tyre, stop as soon as it is safe. Change it only when you can do so without endangering yourself or anyone else. Otherwise, call a breakdown service.

Tyre pressures and wear

Check tyre pressures every week, before a journey and while the tyres are cold. Warm or hot tyres may produce a misleading pressure reading.

Under-inflated or over-inflated tyres adversely affect braking and steering.

Excessive or uneven tyre wear may be caused by:

• braking-system faults
• suspension faults
• incorrect wheel alignment.

Have these faults corrected as soon as possible.

Fluid levels and winter preparation

Check your vehicle’s fluid levels at least weekly. Low brake-fluid levels may cause brake failure and a collision. Know the meaning of any low-fluid warning lights fitted to your vehicle.

Before winter, ensure that the battery is properly maintained and that suitable antifreeze is present in the radiator and windscreen-washer bottle.

Other problems

If the vehicle pulls to one side while braking, the likely cause is a brake fault or incorrectly inflated tyres. Consult a garage or mechanic immediately.

If the vehicle continues bouncing after you push down on its front or rear, its shock absorbers are worn. Worn shock absorbers can seriously impair the vehicle’s operation and should be replaced.

Investigate unusual smells, including burning rubber, petrol or an electrical smell, immediately. Do not risk a fire.

Overheated engines and fires

Most engines are water-cooled. If the engine overheats, allow it to cool naturally. Remove the coolant filler cap and add water or another coolant only after the engine has cooled.

If the vehicle catches fire, get everyone out quickly and move them to a safe place. Do not attempt to extinguish a fire in the engine compartment because opening the bonnet may cause the fire to flare. Call the fire brigade.

Fuel safety

When filling a vehicle’s fuel tank or a fuel can, avoid spilling fuel on the petrol-station forecourt. Report any spillage to the attendant immediately.

Diesel spills are particularly dangerous to motorcyclists because they substantially reduce tyre grip.

Check for fuel leaks and make sure that:

• the fuel tank is not overfilled
• the fuel cap is securely fastened
• the cap seal is not torn, perished or missing
• the fuel cap and tank have no visible damage
• any emergency fuel cap forms a good seal.

Never smoke or use a mobile phone on a petrol-station forecourt. Both present a major fire risk and could cause an explosion.

Commercial vehicles

Complete all daily walkaround checks recommended by the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency and the Fleet Operator Recognition Scheme.

DVSA commercial-vehicle safety
(https://www.gov.uk/dvsa/commercial-vehicle-safety)

Fleet Operator Recognition Scheme
(https://www.fors-online.org.uk)

Vehicle security

Whenever you leave your vehicle:

• remove the ignition key and engage the steering lock
• lock the vehicle, even if leaving it for only a few minutes
• close all windows completely
• never leave children or pets in an unventilated vehicle
• take all contents with you or lock them in the boot
• never leave vehicle documents inside.

A carrier bag may appear to contain valuables and attract a thief even when its contents are unimportant.

For additional security, fit an anti-theft device such as an alarm or immobiliser. When buying a new vehicle, check its built-in security features.

Consider having the vehicle’s registration number etched onto every window. This is an inexpensive and effective deterrent to professional thieves.

category: The Highway Code. 28. Annex 7. First aid on the road
subcategory: 1. Deal with danger. 2. Get help. 3. Help those involved. 4. Provide emergency care
englishSubcategory: 1. Deal with danger. 2. Get help. 3. Help those involved. 4. Provide emergency care
description:
1. Deal with danger

Further collisions and fire are the principal dangers after a crash.

Approach involved vehicles carefully and watch for hazards such as spilled oil and broken glass. Switch off all engines and, if possible, warn other traffic.

If you have a vehicle, switch on its hazard warning lights. Prevent anyone from smoking near the incident. If your first-aid kit contains gloves, put them on.

2. Get help

If it is safe, ask bystanders to help. Ask someone to call the appropriate emergency services on 999 or 112 as soon as possible.

The emergency services will need:

• the incident’s exact location
• the direction of traffic, such as northbound or southbound
• the number of vehicles involved
• information about the casualties’ condition.

Report whether anyone:

• is having difficulty breathing
• is bleeding heavily
• is trapped in a vehicle
• does not respond when spoken to.

3. Help those involved

DO NOT move a casualty from a vehicle unless there is a threat of further danger.

DO NOT remove a motorcyclist’s helmet unless doing so is essential.

DO:

• keep casualties warm, dry and as comfortable as possible
• reassure them calmly and confidently
• try not to leave them alone
• prevent them from wandering into the path of traffic.

DO NOT give casualties anything to eat or drink.

4. Provide emergency care

Remember DRABC: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing and Circulation.

D — Danger

Check that it is safe to approach the casualty.

R — Response

Try to obtain a response by gently shaking the casualty’s shoulders and asking loudly, ‘Are you all right?’ If the casualty responds, check for injuries.

A — Airway

If there is no response, open the airway by placing your fingers under the casualty’s chin and lifting it forwards.

If the casualty is unconscious but breathing, place them in the recovery position until medical assistance arrives.

B — Breathing

Check whether the casualty is breathing normally:

• look for chest movement
• look and listen for breathing
• feel for breath against your cheek.

If there are no signs of breathing, begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR).

For an adult:

• interlock your fingers
• place your hands in the centre of the chest
• press down firmly and quickly
• compress the chest by approximately 5 to 6 centimetres
• give approximately two compressions per second.

For a child, you may need to use only one hand and should not press down as far.

For an infant, use two fingers in the centre of the chest and compress it by approximately one-third of its depth.

Continue CPR until the casualty begins breathing again or a medical professional takes over.

C — Circulation

If the casualty is responsive and breathing, look for bleeding. Protect yourself from contact with blood.

Check whether anything, such as glass, is embedded in the wound. Do not remove an embedded object. Avoid pressing on it and build padding around both sides.

If nothing is embedded, press firmly over the wound to restrict blood loss. As soon as practical, secure a pad over the wound with a bandage or length of cloth. Use the cleanest material available.

Burns

Extinguish any flames while protecting your own safety. Cool a burn for at least 20 minutes using plenty of clean, cool water.

Cover the burn with cling film if it is available. Do not remove anything stuck to the burn.

Be prepared

Always carry a first-aid kit. You may never need it, but it could save a life.

Learn first aid from a qualified organisation such as:

• St John Ambulance
• St Andrew’s First Aid
• the British Red Cross
• another suitably qualified organisation.

category: The Highway Code. 29. Annex 8. Safety code for new drivers
subcategory: The safety code. New Drivers Act. Further training
englishSubcategory: The safety code. New Drivers Act. Further training
description:
The safety code

Many of the most serious collisions happen at night. The period between midnight and 6 am presents a particularly high risk for new drivers. Avoid driving during these hours unless it is genuinely necessary.

Passengers

When carrying passengers, you are responsible for their safety. Do not allow them to distract you or persuade you to take risks. Explain that you need to concentrate to reach the destination safely.

Never show off or attempt to compete with other drivers, particularly when they are driving badly.

Alcohol, drugs and medicines

Do not drive after consuming alcohol or taking drugs.

Even medicines available without a prescription may impair your ability to drive safely. Read the label to find out whether a medicine may affect your driving.

Seat belts

Make sure that everyone in the vehicle wears a seat belt throughout the journey.

Speed and vehicle control

Keep your speed down. Many serious collisions occur because drivers lose control, particularly on bends.

Powerful vehicles

Most new drivers have no experience of high-powered or sporty vehicles. Unless you learned in such a vehicle, gain plenty of experience driving independently before driving a more powerful car.

Insurance

Driving without insurance is an offence. See Annex 3, Motor vehicle documentation and learner driver requirements, for information about the available types of insurance cover.

New Drivers Act

Under the New Drivers Act, your licence will be revoked if you accumulate six penalty points within two years of passing your first driving test.

To regain a full licence, you must pass both the theory test and the practical driving test again.

Further training

Consider additional driver training such as Pass Plus. It can help reduce your risk of being involved in a collision and may also reduce the cost of your insurance.
